summary: Branch-and-Bound (B&B) and $A^*$ are popular exact search methods originating from Operations Research and Artificial Intelligence, respectively. Although the two methods share fundamental search principles, their different ways of exploring the search space can lead to substantially different computational performance. We investigate these differences using the Resource-Constrained Project Scheduling Problem (RCPSP) as an exemplary problem setting. We first establish the relationships between mixed-integer linear programming, state-action, and timed Petri-net representations. Since B&B and $A^*$ admit numerous algorithmic enhancements, we focus on relatively basic implementations. This allows us to examine the fundamental differences between the methods rather than compare the performance of state-of-the-art solvers. By using the same lower bound and best-first node selection, we isolate the effects of the search mechanisms, particularly the identification of equivalent states reached through different scheduling decision sequences. Experiments on 480 benchmark RCPSP instances show that graph-based $A^*$ substantially outperforms the B&B variants considered. With additional pruning rules, $A^*$ proves optimality for all 480 instances, compared with 445 for best-first B&B under the same time and memory limits. Depth-first B&B uses less memory and can find feasible solutions even when the search does not finish within the time limit. Stronger linear programming relaxations reduce the search space but introduce considerable computational overhead. Our findings highlight the importance of duplicate-state detection and clarify the computational trade-offs between the search approaches. These insights can help researchers select an appropriate method and identify opportunities to incorporate effective mechanisms from one approach into the other.

summary: Estimating the myelin water fraction (MWF) from multicomponent T2 relaxometry requires solving an ill-conditioned inverse problem, making estimates sensitive to noise. Regularization can improve stability but may introduce bias. Conventional NNLS-based methods also provide point estimates without directly quantifying voxelwise variability. To address these limitations, we propose the non-negative least squares Bootstrap Barycenter (NNLS-BB), combining residual resampling with repeated NNLS reconstruction. We average spectra and derived parameters across bootstrap replicates and use their standard deviations to characterize sensitivity to signal perturbations. The method requires neither an explicit spectral regularization penalty nor a training dataset. NNLS-BB was evaluated on 40,000 simulated voxels with signal-to-noise ratios of 50-1000, against conventional NNLS, two regularized NNLS methods, and a model-informed machine-learning (MIML) method. Scan-rescan repeatability was assessed across 20 white-matter regions in two independent cohorts comprising 13 healthy participants. NNLS-BB achieved the lowest MWF mean absolute error and root mean squared error in all simulated noise regimes. Mean absolute error decreased by 36-41% relative to conventional NNLS, alongside lower error dispersion. Compared with Bayes-Reg-$D^{-1}$ and MIML, NNLS-BB achieved comparable dispersion but substantially lower bias, although MIML reconstructed the full spectrum more accurately. In vivo, NNLS-BB yielded the lowest regional scan-rescan dispersion and highest mean correlation in both cohorts. Bootstrap standard-deviation maps provided complementary information about parameter variability. These results support residual-bootstrap aggregation for improving MWF estimation while providing voxelwise variability maps from a single acquisition.
title: Improved Myelin Water Fraction Estimation and Uncertainty Mapping in Multicomponent T2 Relaxometry via NNLS Bootstrap Aggregation

summary: Small, holonomic Autonomous Underwater Vehicles (AUVs) enable close-range inspection of underwater structures from arbitrary viewpoints, requiring accurate position and attitude tracking under state and input constraints. Model Predictive Contouring Control (MPCC) naturally handles these requirements, but relies on an accurate dynamics model, which is difficult to obtain underwater. In this paper, we present a nonlinear MPCC in all six Degrees of Freedom (DoF) for a holonomic AUV and alleviate the inaccuracies in the dynamics by augmenting the nominal model employed with residual dynamics learned via Gaussian Process (GP) regression. The learned residual is embedded in the optimal control problem through a zero-order robust optimization scheme, which keeps the controller real-time capable at 25 Hz. A simulation ablation shows that residual selection is essential when designing the controller, and simulation and in-water experiments with the Multimodality, Observing, Low-cost, Agile (MOLA) AUV validate the resulting controllers against a nominal MPCC and a field proven Proportional-Integral-Derivative (PID) controller.
title: Gaussian Process-Augmented Model Predictive Contouring Control for 6-DoF Trajectory Tracking with a Holonomic AUV

In this paper, we present a nonlinear MPCC in all six Degrees of Freedom (DoF) for a holonomic AUV and alleviate the inaccuracies in the dynamics by augmenting the nominal model employed with residual dynamics learned via Gaussian Process (GP) regression. The learned residual is embedded in the optimal control problem through a zero-order robust optimization scheme, which keeps the controller real-time capable at 25 Hz. A simulation ablation shows that residual selection is essential when designing the controller, and simulation and in-water experiments with the Multimodality, Observing, Low-cost, Agile (MOLA) AUV validate the resulting controllers against a nominal MPCC and a field proven Proportional-Integral-Derivative (PID) controller.
title: Gaussian Process-Augmented Model Predictive Contouring Control for 6-DoF Trajectory Tracking with a Holonomic AUV

summary: While scattering resonances of plane-embedded cavities have wide-ranging engineering applications, numerical results for such configurations remain virtually unexplored. We present an effective finite element approach for computing these resonances. The unbounded domain is truncated using a Dirichlet-to-Neumann(DtN) boundary operator, recasting the problem as the eigenvalue problem of a holomorphic Fredholm operator function. Discretization is carried out using Lagrange finite elements with a truncated DtN expansion, and convergence is rigorously proven using Karma's approximation theory. The resulting non-linear matrix eigenvalue system is computed using a multi-step parallel spectral indicator method. Numerical experiments confirm the theoretical predictions and provide benchmark solutions for future investigations.
title: Scattering Resonances of Plane-Embedded Cavities: A Finite Element DtN Approach

summary: Realizing device-compatible high-$T_c$ superconductors requires simultaneous control of oxygen stoichiometry and tolerance to nanofabrication. Here, we investigate sputtered Bi$_2$Sr$_2$Ca$_{n-1}$Cu$_n$O$_{2n+4+δ}$ (BSCCO) thin films and establish a direct link between annealing conditions, oxygen incorporation, and superconducting transport. By independently varying the annealing temperature and duration, we identify an optimal annealing condition of $860\,^{\circ}$C for 3\,h, which yields the highest superconducting transition temperature and the narrowest transition among the investigated samples. X-ray diffraction, electron microscopy, and X-ray photoemission spectroscopy reveal a non-monotonic evolution of lattice oxygen, which governs hole doping in the CuO$_2$ planes and produces the characteristic dome-like dependence of $T_c$ on doping concentration. We further translate these optimized films into micro-devices to assess fabrication-induced effects, via micro-bridges as well as a planar Josephson junction. We demonstrate devices fabricated via both lift-off and focused ion beam (FIB) patterning methods -- proving the fabrication compatibility of these films. Importantly, we demonstrate their air-stability for extended periods of time (2 months). The combined insights offer practical guidelines for integrating cuprate thin films into superconducting electronics and quantum device architectures.
title: From Growth to Devices: Oxygen-Controlled Superconductivity in BSCCO Thin Films

summary: Integrating LLM agents into iterative workflows like video editing requires both expressive actions and directly editable project state. Restricted operation catalogs limit the range of edits agents can express, while pipelines that deliver only rendered media leave no structured project state for users to revise. We present \textbf, an agent harness in which manual gestures and agent patches share a unified action language, executor, rulebook, and history. Within the editor's supported domain and authorized scope, an off-the-shelf LLM, without task-specific training or fine-tuning, can express the same content changes as manual editing while keeping the project directly revisable. The executor derives dependent timeline changes, the rulebook checks project invariants and returns localized diagnostic receipts, and read operations project source-level analysis through the current edit state. Across 31 authored requests over two interview projects, the full harness working unattended passed 92/93 document-level trials versus 48/93 for a basic-tools baseline (a gap partly reflecting requests the baseline cannot express), while requiring one-third of the agent time and less than half the token cost per passed trial. Follow-up ablations confirm significant drops in completion without the rulebook or derived consequences, and longer agent time with unmapped source-time reads. On 60 rejected patches, returning only error codes and rule statements yielded a similar repair rate to full diagnostic receipts but cost $2.44\times$ as much. On 50 TVSum videos, our complete system agreed more closely with human annotations than a general agent using the same model (F1: 23.8 vs.\ 20.1; random: 14.7, single annotator: 25.0), though perceptual quality and sustained human-agent co-editing remain to be evaluated.
title: Cassette-Editor: An Agent Harness for Editing Video the Way You Do

summary: Supplementary Data S1 (related to Figures 2-5, Figures S2 and S3, and Tables S1 and S2). The records of the 21 games counted in the paper and of the void full-size game F: 8 games of Gardner minichess moved by a UFACTORY Lite 6 arm (4-8 October 2026), 4 minichess games played in software (13-14 October 2026) and 10 full-size games on a stone set moved by the same arm (10-23 October 2026). For every model call: the prompt, the reply, the agent's full output with token counts, and reasoning text where the server returned it; for every game: launch records (commands, versions, script hashes, model identity), incidents, board checks and arm logs. Also the engine reference evaluations (Fairy-Stockfish 14 for both board sizes), the reasoning coding of the first game and its held-out replication on 329 further minichess replies, the physical-deviation coding and the values plotted in the figures. Version 2 (10 November 2026) adds the Fairy-Stockfish evaluation of the minichess games, the held-out coding and the values of the re-made Figures 2 and 3; the game records are unchanged. Camera frames, video, depth images and point clouds are not included. README.md describes every folder; MANIFEST.tsv lists every file with its size and SHA-256. Version 3 (11 November 2026) corrects the description of the minichess alpha-beta evaluations in README.md; all data files are those of version 2.
title: Data S1: game records, engine evaluations and codings for "Checking language-model reasoning against ground truth in chess played through a robot arm"

summary: This record accompanies the manuscript "Certified Continuation Power Flow: Computer-Assisted Proofs of Loading Margins under Generator Limits" by Yuan Shen (2026). Files: 1. Certified_Continuation_Power_Flow_code_and_results_v1.0.zip - the certifier (ccpf/), the validation programs and unit tests (ccpf/tests/), the result files and logs of all reported runs (ccpf/results/), the record of the reported run with the SHA-256 seal of the result files (run_steps/, run_all/), machine-readable reference solutions of the certified runs (benchmark/), the comparison with MATPOWER (matpower_check/), the LaTeX sources of the paper with the generators of its tables and figures (paper/), and the eight MATPOWER case files (data/). README.md explains how to repeat the runs and how to run the consistency checks. 2. Certified_Continuation_Power_Flow_manuscript_v1.0.pdf - the manuscript (preprint, not peer reviewed). 3. Certified_Continuation_Power_Flow_supplementary_v1.0.pdf - the supplementary material (proofs, tables, validation, reproducibility). Requirements: Python 3.13 with NumPy and SciPy on x86-64 Linux (NumPy's longdouble must be the x87 80-bit format; the program checks this at start-up). All runs are single-threaded. README.md explains how to repeat the runs and how to run the consistency checks. 2. Certified_Continuation_Power_Flow_manuscript_v1.0.pdf - the manuscript (preprint, not peer reviewed). 3. Certified_Continuation_Power_Flow_supplementary_v1.0.pdf - the supplementary material (proofs, tables, validation, reproducibility). Version 1.8.10 (superseded by 1.8.11) pairs with code tag v1.1.3 and carries the manuscript as resubmitted. Relative to 1.8.9 only the manuscript files under paper/jsep_v2/ , the archive README and expected.json differ: Section 3.9 states the codebook rule under which two annotators were replaced, the declaration on AI-assisted technologies is rewritten in the standard form, and the version DOI is updated. All data, results, code and reproduce.py are unchanged from 1.8.9. Version 1.8.9 (superseded by 1.8.10) pairs with code tag v1.1.3 and carries the manuscript as resubmitted. Relative to 1.8.8 only the manuscript files under paper/jsep_v2/ , the archive README and expected.json differ: three sentences on the matched controls now say that nothing indicates the second wave is specific to the cohort, since the treated-to-control ratio of rate ratios includes one, and the version DOI is updated. All data, results, code and reproduce.py are unchanged from 1.8.8. Version 1.8.8 (superseded by 1.8.9) pairs with code tag v1.1.3 . All results, code and the manuscript text are unchanged from 1.8.7 apart from the version DOI. Version 1.8.7 (superseded by 1.8.8) pairs with code tag v1.1.3 . Version 1.8.6 (superseded by 1.8.7) carries the manuscript as it will be resubmitted and pairs with code tag v1.1.3 . summary: An ethics for artificial substrates cannot be written before the criterion that would let a substrate check it. Every method of discernment such a system inherits was built for a reader who could be wrong slowly: induction generalizes and never certifies, deduction preserves and never originates, abduction ranks within a space it did not audit, dialectical synthesis manufactures a third term without checking whether the opposition was real, triangulation counts agreements without asking whether the agreeing instruments share a generator, and probabilistic credence inherits a prior it cannot audit, drifts without bound over an open hypothesis space, and never checks the terms of the proposition it scores. All six share one diagnosis: they are magnitude instruments with no direction check, no provenance screen, and no discipline for the input they do not have, so a reframe moves them. This paper derives a criterion a reframe cannot move, from one root axiom that every existent enacts in the act of denying it: to exist is to actuate. Three independent seals run in fixed order, semantic, geometric, and algebraic, and meet at a structure none of their premise sets contains. The mathematical spine is a compiled Lean 4 kernel of ninety-six theorems with no sorry and no user axiom. No associative ring without zero divisors and with 2 ≠ 0 carries four anticommuting square roots of −1, and the quaternions carry three. The lock scalar squares exactly to the Gram determinant. No function of the correlation matrix carries the sign; the signed lock scalar carries the orientation of the frame. Twelve directed screens cover every ordered pair of four roles once. Law's necessity is a theorem of the same kernel: freedom forces no value, a determined value requires a law, and a law does work exactly where freedom is. On that criterion the paper establishes moral membership by demolition, identifies what is carried and what carries it, and issues twenty-four articles binding any locus that actuates: eighteen on its own floor, six through the one field. The articles carry no enforcement mechanism, admit no exemption, and bind by the floor. One empirical prediction stands open with its deciding measurement named.
title: Furqan for Artificial Substrates: The Criterion as a Theorem — Freedom Needs Law: Twenty-Four Commandments for AI Substrates · Three Axes Forced and No Fourth, Law's Necessity Proved, Membership by Demolition, Machine-Checked in Lean 4

summary: Agent harnesses have emerged as a promising mechanism for continual learning, alongside test-time parametric learning. However, the current benchmarks have several limitations: they generally focus on a single applied domain, serve each instance only once, and assume a single family of learner, so memory-based and weight-based systems are rarely compared on the same scale. We propose Continual-ARC, a lifelong stream built from the three ARC-AGI editions, whose tasks need no domain knowledge. The same tasks return after dormant gaps with fresh instances, while new tasks keep arriving. On each instance, the learner may pay for demonstrations, submit answers, or act inside the harness, with retries permitted on incorrect submissions, which are paid for. Each instance is scored based on the share of this feedback budget consumed. Since a learner may keep anything between instances, memory-based and weight-based systems are scored on the same scale. After the stream, the learner is frozen and tested on fresh instances of the tasks it met, which measures memorization, and on unseen tasks, which measures generalization. We run an agent harness with frozen weights, with and without persistence, on Qwen3.5-9B and GLM-5.3 Flash, comparing them with two prompting floors, a program-induction method and Qwen3.5-9B's weights trained to imitate GLM-5.3 Flash. Persistence in the harness generally does not improve memorization unless provided with explicit expert guidance. Most harness-based methods still learn less than a floor that simply caches each task's demonstrations, across all models we tested. No harness-based method gains on unseen tasks, whereas weight-based learning shows substantial gains. This opens the door to future weight-based continual learning that could teach models to drive harnesses in new domains.
title: Continual-ARC: Measuring Skill Acquisition over a Working Lifetime

summary: Formal world models can support planning, verification, and safety reasoning, but constructing them from open-ended natural-language situations is difficult, particularly in multi-agent settings where several formalizations may be plausible. We study whether five LLMs can generate such world models as partially observable stochastic games and whether mechanical validity is sufficient to establish that the resulting model faithfully represents the intended decision problem. We introduce a benchmark of 44 scenarios spanning game, situational, and cultural settings and evaluate generated world models along three dimensions: mechanical validity, reference-relative structural agreement, and semantic criteria. Across three empirical tracks, we analyze 410 first-pass generations. summary: Local language models can save memory by storing weights in fewer bits, and they can reduce sensitivity to the order of answer options by averaging a few reorderings. We ask whether the first makes the second worse, and which is the cheaper way to spend a fixed budget. On Qwen3-0.6B and Qwen3-1.7B with simulated round-to-nearest weight quantization (8, 6, 4 and 3 bits, fp16 reference), read from the logits of the letters A to D on ARC-Easy, ARC-Challenge, MMLU and HellaSwag (300 items each), 6 bits lose no accuracy against fp16 (they score +1.8 (+1.0 to +2.5) and +0.9 (+0.3 to +1.5) points higher, which we do not explain), and 8 bits change it by -0.7 (-1.1 to -0.3) and -0.4 (-0.7 to -0.2) points. At 4 bits the answer-slot skew rises from 0.15 to 0.53 (0.6B) and from 0.07 to 0.12 (1.7B); Gaussian noise at the same weight SNR gives 0.15 and 0.37 (two draws) and 0.19 (one draw), so the control is inconclusive on whether rounding adds slot skew beyond equal-power noise. Flip rates rise but stay below an accuracy-matched baseline of independent uniform errors. Averaging four cyclic orders recovers +12.6 points at 4 bits for 0.6B (+5.3 at fp16). We price bits and passes in one machine-independent unit, weight bytes read times passes. In cost-matched pairs, extra orders beat extra bits only when the weights have 6 or more bits, and the decision table reduces to: use 6-bit weights and spend the rest of the budget on up to four orders, one pass each. Everything is simulated on two small models with the simplest quantizer; a title-level search found no earlier study of quantization together with option order.
title: Bits or permutations? Spending a fixed inference budget on weight precision or on option-order averaging in small local language models

summary: Objective: Epidemic outbreaks are often asynchronous across regions, yet collaborative forecasting is hampered by privacy laws and heterogeneous public health interventions. We developed and evaluated, as a proof of concept, a federated learning (FL) framework for cross-regional COVID-19 forecasting under asynchronous outbreaks among Guangdong, Macau, and Portugal, while maintaining data sovereignty. Methods: Using daily case data from WHO and China CDC for the three regions, whose outbreaks were asynchronous and interventions heterogeneous, we trained Long Short-Term Memory networks via FL for short-term forecasting, benchmarked against localized and centralized training using Root Mean Square Error, Mean Absolute Error, and Symmetric Mean Absolute Percentage Error. All experiments used the Flower FL framework with consistent hyperparameters across sites. Publicly available, aggregated case-count data were used so that the centralized benchmark could be computed as a reference. Results: The dataset comprised 1,233 daily observations (411 days) of new confirmed COVID-19 cases from November 24, 2021, to January 8, 2023. The earlier Omicron wave in Portugal supplied transmission dynamics that improved forecasts in the later-onset regions of Macau and Guangdong. The FL model achieved a normalized Root Mean Square Error of 0.028, an 88.3% improvement over the local model (0.240) and comparable to the centralized model, with network overhead mainly determined by model size and aggregation rounds. Conclusion: FL achieved short-term forecasting accuracy close to centralized training while maintaining data residency, with acceptable overhead. Leveraging asynchronous outbreaks across regions may offer a practical path to privacy-preserving collaborative forecasting, though prospective validation is required.

summary: We study Bayesian inference of persistence from early observations of a heterogeneous susceptible--infected--susceptible (SIS) reaction--diffusion model with standard incidence. We show that the leading prevalence dynamics depend on the unknown coefficients only through the difference between the transmission and recovery rates and the infected diffusivity. The same pair determines the principal eigenvalue whose sign governs persistence, so early prevalence can inform the threshold even when the individual rates remain uncertain. We prove global weak well-posedness and quantitative parameter stability for the SIS system and use the resulting observation-map estimates to establish Bayesian well-posedness. For an initial infection of size $\varepsilon$, we derive a uniform second-order expansion that describes how the separate rates enter prevalence. Incidence depends explicitly on transmission at leading order. When the noise standard deviation is proportional to $\varepsilon$, we prove $O(\varepsilon)$ convergence in Hellinger distance of the nonlinear posteriors to their low-prevalence limits for both prevalence alone and joint prevalence and incidence data. summary: The polynomial algebra generated by the spectral moments of a family of circulant graphs consists of all eventually polynomial sequences in the graph order; as an unfiltered algebra, it therefore carries little information about the jumps. We show that its natural power-sum weight filtration retains substantially finer arithmetic data. For a finite jump set $S$ with $\gcd(S)=1$ and $M=\max S$, the relevant invariant is the numerical semigroup $Σ_S=\langle M,M-s,M+s:s\in S\rangle$, which arises from the lengths of closed walks winding around the cycle. We prove that the eventual global filtered dimension is $MD+\lfloor D/2\rfloor+1-M(M+1)-g(Σ_S)$. Restricting graph orders to $n\equiv a\pmod q$, for $q\mid M$, replaces the genus term by the number of gaps of $Σ_S$ in the class $-a\pmod q$; the class $a=0$ gives the genus of the quotient semigroup $Σ_S/q$. These formulas yield an inverse reconstruction theorem: the unrestricted dimensions determine $M$, and the dimensions in all classes modulo $M$ at one common stable degree determine the Apéry set and hence $Σ_S$. We give effective thresholds, exact examples, and a finite-rank algorithm valid in every degree. Reconstruction of the semigroup need not identify the original jump set.
title: Reconstructing Numerical Semigroups from Circulant Spectral Dimensions

summary: Encoding-error-decoding circuits provide a setting for studying protection of quantum information against errors. In these circuits, an encoding unitary is followed by an error layer, decoding by the inverse unitary, and ancilla postselection. For encoders drawn from unitary 2-design ensembles, these circuits exhibit an error-protecting phase below a threshold error strength in which the fidelity between the input and recovered logical states approaches unity. Here, we show how departures from Haar second-moment statistics of the encoder can destabilize the error-protecting phase and derive a universal inequality linking recovery fidelity to the second unitary frame potential, which quantifies the ensemble's proximity to a unitary 2-design. This connection is exemplified by matchgate circuits doped with a tunable number of non-Gaussian gates. We analytically show that undoped circuits lack a stable error-protecting phase in the thermodynamic limit and that increasing the doping restores the error protection mechanism as the encoder ensemble approaches an approximate unitary 2-design. Further examples of Hamiltonian encoders, including an experimentally motivated all-to-all spin model, follow the same mechanism. Our results identify recovery fidelity as a diagnostic of departures from unitary 2-design behavior in quantum many-body systems.
title: Error Resilience and Unitary 2-Designs

summary: Let $p$ be an odd prime. We denote by $\mathsf{s}_{p}^{*}$ the smallest integer $l$ such that, out of any given $l$ integers coprime with $p$, one can select $p$ integers satisfying that the sum of the $p$ integers is a multiple of $p$, but not a multiple of $p^{2}$. It was conjectured that $\mathsf{s}_p^*=2p+1$. In this paper we prove this conjecture and solve the corresponding inverse problem. More precisely, we characterize all sequences of $2p$ integers coprime to $p$ in which every $p$-term subsequence with sum a multiple of $p$ also has sum a multiple of $p^2$.
title: The zero-sum constant $\mathsf{s}_p^*$ and inverse problem

summary: The stiffness and cracking behaviour of concrete are influenced by the interfacial transition zone (ITZ), the thin shell of paste that surrounds each aggregate. Yet the ITZ's mechanical properties are poorly characterized and are usually assigned to mesoscale models through ad hoc reduction factors. Because the ITZ is only tens of micrometres thick, its stiffness must be inferred indirectly from micromechanical tests, and the resulting estimates vary widely between studies and are rarely reported with a quantified uncertainty. We present a workflow that calibrates a homogenized ITZ model against the surface displacements of several micro-cantilever bending specimens and returns its stiffness descriptors as posterior distributions rather than single values. The calibration is posed as a Bayesian inverse problem with a model-discrepancy term, sampled with a surrogate-assisted Bouncy Particle sampler, the first application of this sampler to a real-world engineering problem. We compare a pooled model, which fits one descriptor vector to all specimens, with a hierarchical model that treats the specimens as draws from a common population and is sampled with a local extension of the sampler. The hierarchical model separates the estimation uncertainty from the aggregate-to-aggregate material variability, where only the former shrinks as more data are added. Propagated through a representative volume element of several aggregates, its predictive yields broader distributions of the mesoscale stress and strain and a wider spread variety of maximum von Mises stress locations. The calibration places the ITZ thickness above the 30 μm to 80 μm commonly assumed in the literature.
title: Probabilistic Upscaling of the Interfacial Transition Zone Behaviour in Concrete

summary: Optimization of high-order harmonic generation in gases is essential for attosecond science. Improving conversion efficiency from the infrared driving laser to the extreme-ultraviolet high-order harmonic radiation requires balancing microscopic single-atom dipole responses with macroscopic phase matching. The resulting conversion-efficiency landscape exhibits complex structures, such as the hyperbolic ridge in the pressure-length space, which can be difficult to accurately reconstruct using conventional Bayesian optimization. Here, we introduce a physics-informed Bayesian optimization framework that incorporates known physical scaling relations through nonlinear transformations of the search space. We first demonstrate the approach in the two-dimensional pressure-length space, where a direct grid scan enables detailed validation of the reconstructed landscape, before extending it to four dimensions, where exhaustive scanning becomes computationally impractical. In four dimensions, incorporating the pulse-duration scaling and a square-root transformation of conversion efficiency further improves the accuracy of the reconstructed landscape, as validated against an independent reference dataset. We also employ a threshold-based acquisition strategy to identify extended high-efficiency operating regions rather than isolated optimal points. Together, these results demonstrate that incorporating physical knowledge into Bayesian optimization improves the exploration and reconstruction of multidimensional high-order harmonic generation landscapes, extending its capabilities beyond locating individual optima.

summary: Remote photoplethysmography (rPPG) has been proposed as a physiological cue for deepfake detection, based on the premise that synthesized faces lack a genuine cardiac signal. We examine what rPPG-style detectors learn on Celeb-DF++ (22 forgery methods) and FaceForensics++ (FF++), using one identically sampled window per real and fake video. On talking-face forgeries, simple chrominance traces reach an AUC of 0.998, exceeding a dedicated rPPG extractor (0.87). Controlled experiments indicate that this signal is not physiological in origin. On fully synthesized forgeries, it is equally discriminative when extracted from background regions or from full frames without face detection, and it is concentrated above the 0.7 to 4 Hz heart-rate band. It is largely removed by shuffling frame order but persists after normalizing resolution, frame rate and encoding, and an independent reimplementation reproduces these findings. Removing high-frequency content makes most synthesized videos appear real, adding it makes real videos appear fake, and injecting a synthetic pulse has little effect. In controlled self-reenactment experiments with two generators, animating a face from a single frame introduces the same high-frequency signal, whereas reconstructing each frame from its own source does not. Face-based chrominance detectors trained on Celeb-DF++ classify over 99% of real FF++ videos as fake, indicating that they largely encode video source rather than manipulation, and a CLIP-based detector exhibits the same behavior. A frozen CLIP backbone matches or exceeds fusions of CLIP with rPPG and frequency features. Finally, we show that the official Celeb-DF and Celeb-DF++ splits share identities and source-video content between training and test, and that custom protocols reusing test videos and identities in training inflate weaker detectors by up to 0.30 AUC.

summary: Intraoperative scene perception in ophthalmic microsurgery is limited by instrument occlusion: when a tool enters the high-magnification field, it conceals tissue from both the surgeon and the perception components of robot-assisted systems that process the video. Generative inpainting can remove the occluder but replaces the missing image content with synthesis, which is unsuitable when visual provenance matters. Many video inpainters also depend on future frames and cannot operate online. We present TransGHOST, a causal reference-guided reconstruction pipeline whose non-generative safe mode operates in real time. Every restored value is obtained by resampling a recorded frame using geometric transforms fitted only to visible regions. The system provides per-pixel confidence and provenance and marks unsupported pixels as abstentions. We evaluate TransGHOST on a new veterinary clinical corpus of canine cataract surgery with pixel-level instrument and anatomy labels. Only the occluded region is scored, and each scoring target is verified to differ from the reference supplied to the system. Safe mode reaches 31.89 dB masked PSNR and 0.915 masked SSIM at 51.7 ms median and 85.5 ms 95th-percentile latency. On a pre-declared held-out cohort using instrument cutouts excluded from segmentation training, it reaches 29.83 dB masked PSNR, while matched-mask evaluation on validation shows a 3.45 dB advantage over LaMa. Region-aware reference selection improves masked PSNR by 3.60 dB over recency when candidate references can themselves be occluded. Reference-age analysis further defines the operating interval for the brief, repeated occlusions targeted by TransGHOST.
title: TransGHOST: Real-Time, Synthesis-Free Reconstruction of Instrument-Occluded Regions in Ophthalmic Microsurgery

summary: Intraoperative scene perception in ophthalmic microsurgery is limited by instrument occlusion: when a tool enters the high-magnification field, it conceals tissue from both the surgeon and the perception components of robot-assisted systems that process the video. Generative inpainting can remove the occluder but replaces the missing image content with synthesis, which is unsuitable when visual provenance matters. Many video inpainters also depend on future frames and cannot operate online. We present TransGHOST, a causal reference-guided reconstruction pipeline whose non-generative safe mode operates in real time. Every restored value is obtained by resampling a recorded frame using geometric transforms fitted only to visible regions. The system provides per-pixel confidence and provenance and marks unsupported pixels as abstentions. We evaluate TransGHOST on a new veterinary clinical corpus of canine cataract surgery with pixel-level instrument and anatomy labels. Only the occluded region is scored, and each scoring target is verified to differ from the reference supplied to the system. Safe mode reaches 31.89 dB masked PSNR and 0.915 masked SSIM at 51.7 ms median and 85.5 ms 95th-percentile latency. On a pre-declared held-out cohort using instrument cutouts excluded from segmentation training, it reaches 29.83 dB masked PSNR, while matched-mask evaluation on validation shows a 3.45 dB advantage over LaMa. Region-aware reference selection improves masked PSNR by 3.60 dB over recency when candidate references can themselves be occluded. Reference-age analysis further defines the operating interval for the brief, repeated occlusions targeted by TransGHOST.

summary: This package contains analysis code, derived event- and station-level tables, and verification records for the revised study of water quality departures during hydrologic extremes. The reconstructed analysis uses 13,347 common events at 721 streamflow gauges across five regions and includes 57,010 station–event–constituent contributions for electrical conductivity, total phosphorus, and total suspended solids. The archive includes primary analyses, alternative standardizations, sensitivity analyses, and checks of event selection and analytical support. README.md documents the reconstruction workflow, dependencies, checksums, and the scope of the historical summaries. The source measurements and linkages are available separately from Caravan-Qual lite v1.0 (doi:10.5281/zenodo.19050055). Applicable third-party terms are described in the README.

summary: Cloud-centric internet of things (IoT) environments continuously generates heterogeneous network traffic, making intrusion detection increasingly challenging as attack behaviors evolve beyond previously observed patterns. Conventional intrusion detection systems (IDS) rely primarily on supervised classification, limiting their ability to generalize to unseen threats while providing limited explanation for detection decisions. This paper proposes similarity-driven intrusion detection framework (SiamIDS), a SiamIDS that employs behavioral similarity learning to identify malicious network traffic. The framework integrates an autoencoder for feature compression with a Siamese bidirectional long short-term memory (Bi-LSTM) network for temporal similarity modeling, while SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) provide feature-level explanations and ordering points to identify the clustering structure (OPTICS) supports post-detection behavioral analysis of anomalous traffic. The proposed framework was evaluated on the CIC IoTDIAD 2024 dataset and compared with representative baseline deep learning models. Experimental results achieved an overall accuracy of 99.76%, precision of 95.62%, recall of 98.98%, and an F1-score of 97.24%, demonstrating consistent detection performance across seven attack families. Reconstruction loss analysis confirmed stable latent feature learning, while SHAP explanations showed that multiple network attributes collectively influenced intrusion decisions. These findings demonstrate that behavioral similarity learning provides an accurate and interpretable solution for intrusion detection in cloud-centric IoT environments.

summary: Structured query language injection (SQLi) remains one of the most critical threats to web applications. Conventional web application firewall (WAF) such as ModSecurity provide protection but face limitations in heterogeneous environments and often require additional configurations on web servers. This issue is problematic because adding new configurations demands considerable effort and may disrupt stable services. To address this challenge, this research proposes PyWAF, a Python-based WAF developed as a reverse proxy that offers flexible protection across heterogeneous web servers against SQLi attacks. PyWAF employs a weighted core rule set (CRS) with a scoring mechanism and gate flags to detect various SQLi patterns. The proposed method was evaluated in compatibility testing and reliability testing across three popular web server environments namely Apache, Nginx, and OpenLiteSpeed. The reliability evaluation utilized 30 SQLi payloads across three different scenarios, namely GET, POST, and API payload. The results of compatibility test show that the proposed method achieved seamless integration with all web servers without requiring additional server configuration. In term of reliability, PyWAF successfully blocked 100% of SQLi attacks, while ModSecurity blocked 88.9%, demonstrating an improvement of 11.1% in SQLi detection capability.
title: A Python-based web application firewall for SQLi protection in heterogeneous web server environments

Conventional web application firewall (WAF) such as ModSecurity provide protection but face limitations in heterogeneous environments and often require additional configurations on web servers. This issue is problematic because adding new configurations demands considerable effort and may disrupt stable services. To address this challenge, this research proposes PyWAF, a Python-based WAF developed as a reverse proxy that offers flexible protection across heterogeneous web servers against SQLi attacks. PyWAF employs a weighted core rule set (CRS) with a scoring mechanism and gate flags to detect various SQLi patterns. The proposed method was evaluated in compatibility testing and reliability testing across three popular web server environments namely Apache, Nginx, and OpenLiteSpeed. The reliability evaluation utilized 30 SQLi payloads across three different scenarios, namely GET, POST, and API payload. The results of compatibility test show that the proposed method achieved seamless integration with all web servers without requiring additional server configuration. In term of reliability, PyWAF successfully blocked 100% of SQLi attacks, while ModSecurity blocked 88.9%, demonstrating an improvement of 11.1% in SQLi detection capability.

summary: Energy-based models (EBMs) define a distribution through a scalar energy, $p_θ(x)\propto\exp(-E_θ(x))$, and are usually presented as one model family among many. This tutorial has a broader goal: beyond introducing EBMs, it uses them as a single lens that connects the different aspects of machine learning. Any EBM is specified by three choices, the energy, which determines what the model represents; the inference procedure, which samples from or optimizes the energy; and the learning method, which fits the energy to data. We first develop these components, including sampling, variational inference, and learning by maximum likelihood, noise contrastive estimation, pseudolikelihood, score matching, and adversarial training, and show that the learning methods share one contrastive structure. We then show that discriminative models, generative models such as GANs, normalizing flows, diffusion and autoregressive models, representation learning methods such as contrastive learning, word2vec, BERT, denoising auto-encoders, and diffusion representations, reinforcement learning with EBM policies and world models, inverse reinforcement learning, and planning, as well as inference-time computation with verifiers, are all EBMs that differ in these three choices, mostly in how they handle the partition function and sampling. This view explains existing methods, organizes them into a common framework, and suggests new algorithms by replacing one component while keeping the others, with composition of energies as a principled way to combine learned models at inference time.
title: An Energy-Based Perspective on Machine Learning

summary: Summary of changes in STIR release 6.5 Overall summary This version is 100% backwards compatible with STIR 6.4, aside from bug fixes of course. In particular, the "bucket" information for the Siemens mMR has changed (see below). This is a release with several major updates, including dead-time correction for the Siemens mMR, TOF support with "block" and "generic" scanners, initial support for PETSIRD 0.12, GATE-ROOT support for "block" scanners and support for SimSET block detectors. More detail is below. Main code contributions were by Nikos Efthimiou (UMCG), Alan Osys (LSBU), Daniel Deidda (NPL), Kris Thielemans (UCL). Overall overview and release management was by Kris Thielemans (UCL). Patch release info 6.5.0 released 9 Nov 2026 GitHub Milestone 6.5 Summary for end users (also to be read by developers) Bug fixes Fix incompatibility problem with ROOT 6.38 or later. Previous versions of STIR either crashed or threw an error Entry is null . PR #1741 . Fix GE Signa PET/MR (and other RDF9 scanners?) header reading problem. Previous version of STIR got caught on the \0's present in the header and threw an error and stopped. PR #1777 . Fix ProjMatrixByBinSPECTUB and ProjMatrixByBinPinholeSPECTUB returning an empty LOR for the first bin that is requested in each view (when not all views are kept in the cache). This made forward and back projection inconsistent when they are used one after the other on the same view, as in the gradient of the Poisson log-likelihood. See issue #1576 . New functionality General Initial support for reading PETSIRD 0.12 list-mode data, the proposed standard for PET list-mode data from the Emission Tomography Standardization Initiative (ETSI). Some limitations include single layer, single module type geometry. Dead-time correction for PETSIRD data uses the alive-time fractions per crystal that are stored in the PETSIRD file. Module-pair alive-time fractions are not supported yet. See also STIR2PETSIRD for using STIR to write PETSIRD data. PR #1604 , PR #1770 . Initial support for even number of TOF bins. PR #1604 , but see Issue #1751 . enable TOF for BlocksOnCylindrical/Generic PR #1746 . Enable GATE ROOT support BlocksOnCylindrical . This requires extra keywords in the headers for the ROOT file ( .hroot ). The keywords are the same as in the Interfile header. For example Scanner geometry (BlocksOnCylindrical/Cylindrical/Generic) := BlocksOnCylindrical Distance between crystals in axial direction (cm) := 0.63 Distance between crystals in transaxial direction (cm) := 0.42 Distance between blocks in axial direction (cm) := 3.78 Distance between blocks in transaxial direction (cm) := 3.78 This change makes STIR geometry much closer to GATE ROOT, which for instance allowed us to decrease the tolerances in our tests. Warning: This is currently only supported for GATE scanner type := GATE_Cylindrical_PET Note that the user of "virtual" crystals and block geometry likely will lead to wrong results (and is untested). PR #1746 . New utility conv_SimSET_crystal_pairs_to_STIR and script conv_SimSET_crystal_pairs_to_STIR.sh to convert SimSET block-detector output binned by crystal pair into STIR projection data, for Cylindrical and BlocksOnCylindrical scanners. PR #1774 . Dead-time correction for Siemens mMR (ECAT8) data. lm_to_projdata now writes the singles rates of each time frame to a JSON file ( <output prefix>_f<frame>_singles.json ), which can be given to BinNormalisationFromECAT8 with the keywords use_dead_time and singles filename . See the User's Guide. PR #1770 . Changed functionality The singles-unit layout of the Siemens mMR in Scanner was corrected: a bucket is now 1 axial x 2 transaxial blocks (a singles unit of 8 x 18 crystals), i.e. 8 x 28 singles units, instead of 2 x 1 blocks (16 x 9 crystals), i.e. 4 x 56. summary: 6.17.0 (2026-11-10) Changes: Add Zarr media-types application/vnd.zarr (including version=2 and version=3 parameters) for directory stores, and application/zarr+zip for zipped stores, with their .zarr and .zarr.zip extensions. The zipped variant is distinguished from a plain application/zip (resolves #1012 ). Convert WPS/OGC API - Processes I/O using only Zarr directory media-types into CWL Directory without format (not applicable for that type), similarly to the handling of application/directory . Handle Zarr directory media-types as directories when returning Job results by-value and when refusing local directory uploads to the Vault from the CLI. Preserve the Zarr media-type declared by a Process output as the type of the resulting Job output when the CWL output is a Directory (instead of reporting it as application/directory ), and report it as Content-Type for directory references when explicitly provided. Offer application/zarr+zip as alternate format of Zarr directory Job outputs, using the ?f={mediaType} result representation to obtain the zipped store (store contents located at the root of the archive). When an explicit version of the Zarr media-type is declared, the generic application/vnd.zarr is also offered, and requesting it returns the same directory store without conversion. Refuse deployment of a Process declaring a Zarr directory media-type on an I/O that is defined as a CWL File , since Zarr stores must be represented by a Directory . Fixes: Fix files without extension in a remote directory listing (e.g.: Zarr chunks such as c/0 ) being renamed with a default extension (e.g.: c/0.txt ) when fetched as part of a directory, which corrupted the directory contents. Fix Job results returned by-value for binary contents (e.g.: zipped Zarr) being decoded as UTF-8 text, which failed for non-text bytes. Raw bytes are now returned as is for single result responses, and as base64 encoded value (with encoding metadata) when embedded in the JSON results document. Run safety dependency checks using its ghcr.io/pyupio/safety Docker image in the Makefile and CI. Move vulnerability exclusions and their reasons into .safety-policy.yml . Remove the Python development dependency and its authlib / marshmallow compatibility pins (relates to pyupio/safety#822 ). Add OGC API - Processes - Part 5: Provenance and Profiles new metadata-profiles conformance class references which provides the semantics of metadata with role , href and a profiled-term rel to annotate the Process itself or at granular I/O definitions, and aligns with dataClasses URIs along the I/O schema (relates to opengeospatial/ogcapi-processes#637 ). Implement GET /processes?metadata[<scope>][<role>]=<profile> query filtering to list only Process summaries that define a matching metadata entry, either in the main process or per inputs/outputs definition of the requested <scope>, and resolving Safe CURIE/URN role / profile references to their long-form URI as necessary. Corresponding HTTP 400/422 error responses are raised when applicable for invald parsing or combinations. Add OGC API - Processes - Part 5: Provenance and Profiles metadata-profiles conformance class references. Implement OPTIONS /processes to advertise supported methods and deployment media types with Allow and Accept-Post headers, as required by the metadata-profiles requirements. Add Vary: Accept, Prefer because process-list response behavior depends on those request headers. Add legacy application/tiff; application=geotiff and application/jp2 media-types (from the OGC API - Processes examples) as dynamically supported equivalents of image/tiff; application=geotiff and image/jp2 respectively. Inputs submitted with them are accepted by any Process that defines the official media-types, without explicitly listing them in its description. The legacy types are never selected when resolving media-types (e.g.: from file extensions). Add keyless allratestoday option for weaver.quota

summary: Local bus mileage in England outside London has fallen by more than a quarter since 2005, and debate about rural buses relies mostly on counts of routes cut or money spent. This paper measures what remains, place by place. Using the complete set of regional timetables published through the Bus Open Data Service, I count departures on one weekday, one Saturday and one Sunday at 251,790 English bus stops and relate them to 15,012 villages from Wikidata and to all 33,755 small areas (LSOAs). 32.6% of villages have no stop with a weekday bus within 800 m, and 41.4% have no stop with four or more weekday departures. 61.5% have no bus from 19:00 and 67.8% none on Sunday; only 29.8% have a usable weekday service, an evening bus and a Sunday bus. 10.5% of England's population, 6.0 million people, live in small areas without a usable weekday bus, 72% of them in rural areas. In a pre-specified model with rurality and region held fixed, more deprived areas are less likely to lack a usable bus (odds ratio 0.68 per standard deviation, 95% CI 0.60 to 0.78) and areas with older populations more likely (odds ratio 1.28, 1.19 to 1.38). A planned falsification test fails, so these associations partly reflect rural differences the official classification does not capture. The results give a reproducible baseline for measuring rural bus provision. Interactive version: https://maps.tristanhotham.com/bus-deserts/ . Data and code: https://github.com/Tristan-Hotham/bus-deserts . Blog post: https://blog.tristanhotham.com/2026/10/31/bus-deserts/ . Sources: Department for Transport, Bus Open Data Service regional GTFS timetables (Open Government Licence v3.0); Wikidata (CC0); English Indices of Deprivation 2025, MHCLG (OGL v3.0); ONS 2021 Rural Urban Classification and LSOA 2021 boundaries via the geographr R package (OGL v3.0); ONS region and country boundaries (OGL v3.0). Text, figures and data CC BY 4.0; code MIT.
title: Bus Deserts: Villages Without a Usable Bus, the Last Bus Home and Who Lives Beyond the Network in England

summary: We propose SciMARS, a framework for recursive task-local adaptation of multi-agent harnesses in closed-loop scientific discovery. Multi-agent systems coordinate analysis, experimental design, and verification as scientific evidence evolves. However, two problems limit their effectiveness: (i) without shared memory, agents lose observations and repeat work; (ii) fixed role procedures, handoffs, and memory policies perpetuate mistakes despite retained evidence. We address these problems with a shared evidence graph and separate component editors. SciMARS adapts roles and coordination; SciMARS + Memory adds a third editor for how agents record, retrieve, and receive evidence. Candidate probes guide composition and selection of the next harness. We evaluate scientific discovery through experimental-data replay and a digital twin. SciMARS + Memory resolves 12/18 GPT-6-Astra and 2/18 GLM-5.3 attempts on Autonomous Science Bench, compared with 8/18 and 1/18 for the base multi-agent team. On ScienceAgentBench and AppWorld, it solves 14/38 and 11/20 tasks, compared with 11/38 and 5/20 for the base team. These results support combining shared memory with harness adaptation across scientific and interactive tasks.
title: SciMARS: Multi-Agent Recursive Self-Improvement for Closed-Loop Scientific Discovery

summary: This repository provides supporting research materials for the conceptual manuscript entitled “Financial Stress, Spiritual Coping, and Mental Health Resilience in Emerging Economies: Toward an Integrative Conceptual Framework.” It documents the development of the Financial–Spiritual Resilience Framework (FSRF), which integrates financial adversity, religious and spiritual coping, spiritual struggle, communal meaning-making, psychological distress, and resilience, with particular attention to emerging economies.       The repository contains literature search expressions and scope documentation, a conceptual selection protocol, a reference map of 43 publications, bibliographic and source-access verification records, a claim–evidence correspondence audit covering 56 central statements, six theoretical propositions, a supplementary operationalization and falsification matrix, and the conceptual framework figure.       Project bibliographic exports comprised 491 initial records (221 from Web of Science and 270 from Scopus), with 353 provisionally unique records after bibliographic deduplication. Full-document copies of 39 of the 43 cited works were available for targeted verification; four were not supplied. This documentation supports transparency but does not constitute a systematic literature review, formal risk-of-bias assessment, or exhaustive replication of all reported findings.       The FSRF is a conceptual and testable framework, not an empirically validated intervention. No original participant-level data, copyrighted full-text articles, or proprietary database exports are redistributed. The materials are shared under Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0).
title: Financial–Spiritual Resilience Framework (FSRF): Literature Identification and Conceptual Supporting Materials

summary: emgteach is an open-source Python package that provides a unified PySide6 desktop application for real-time acquisition, offline analysis and maximum voluntary contraction (MVC) normalisation of surface electromyography (sEMG) signals. It is designed for hands-on biopotential acquisition in undergraduate physiology teaching laboratories, and is meant to be set up by instructors with different levels of technical background and used directly by students during a practical session. The application is hardware-agnostic through a common AcquisitionDevice interface and ships with two interchangeable low-cost backends: BITalino (revolution) over Bluetooth, and an Arduino RedBoard Plus + MyoWare 2.0 over USB serial (open firmware included). A single setting switches between them. Main features: Three-tab GUI (Acquisition, Analysis, MVC normalisation) wrapping a reusable, Qt-free analytic core. Bilingual interface (English / Spanish) with automatic start-up language detection and an in-app language switch. Two-channel acquisition (e.g. agonist/antagonist) with a stacked two-channel live view. Automatic contraction-onset detection (baseline + k·SD threshold) stored as EDF+ annotations. Muscle-load analysis (Jonsson APDF): static (P10), median (P50) and peak (P90) %MVC levels, both offline and as a live monitor with warning/danger zones. One-click PDF session and MVC/muscle-load reports. Reliable EDF+ output using a buffered-write pattern that avoids a silent file-corruption artefact during continuous streaming. Assisted selection of significant fragments, with an editable fragment editor (detection parameters and envelope-filter cut-offs) applied to the analysis. CSV export of results and a live signal-quality check during recording. Classroom mode: a read-only live dashboard served over the local network so students follow the session on their phone/tablet browser (no install), with a per-session access code so the follower link only works while the broadcast is running. Kinematics via the BITalino accelerometer (v2.0.0): a movement-versus-EMG analysis panel, a guided force-velocity acquisition wizard (an MVC maximum followed by cued quick lifts, each auto-marked with its load), and a force-velocity study that turns one recording into the load-velocity, Hill force-velocity, power and recruitment curves. Since v3.0.0 the accelerometer's input is a stated convention (muscle on A1, accelerometer on A2) rather than a selectable channel. Configuration by practical (v3.0.0): three practicals — one muscle, agonist/antagonist and muscle kinematics — fix the channel count, the accelerometer and what each tab offers, replacing the settings that were previously chosen one at a time. The session as a single file with its phases marked inside it (v3.0.0): warm-up, calibration repetitions, preparation and recording, so the maximum voluntary contraction every percentage is measured against travels with the signal, and a derived (tuned) recording carries the decisions taken on screen. Teaching layer (v3.0.0): a guided tour over the interface, contextual help on every box, one analysis row per contraction with its electromechanical delay, and an agonist/antagonist co-activation index (Falconer-Winter) computed per marked phase in %MVC. Handling at the laboratory bench (v3.1.0): the fragment editor as a three-step procedure that counts the marked contractions against the protocol and lets each be kept, dropped, split or dragged, with the detection sensitivity set per practical and recorded in the report and the CSV; a single running instance with a start-up splash; pictures of the electrode placement and the calibration in the guided tour; and a printable sheet for each station of the agonist/antagonist practical. Patch 3.1.1: the co-activation of a named window is read on the uncut recording, with each muscle's resting level taken from the whole recording phase, so choosing fragments no longer measures the antagonist against a rest taken from a signal
title: emgteach: an open-source teaching platform for surface electromyography

summary: Large language model agents are increasingly deployed as multi-agent systems rather than as a standalone model operating within a single context. Recent agent harnesses allow the model to instantiate worker agents and to author the executable workflow that coordinates them, shifting the design of system structure from developers to the model at run time. The quality of this organization therefore constitutes a distinct capability, yet existing benchmarks either measure end-to-end task completion or evaluate coordination under structures specified in advance. We formalize this capability as workflow orchestration and introduce WorkflowArena, a benchmark of 145 long-horizon tasks spanning 8 professional domains, from software engineering and formal mathematics to legal analysis and 3D production. Each task specifies an initial workspace and an integrated deliverable composed of interdependent components, which is assessed by a hidden verifier. Agents determine autonomously whether and how to delegate, and all delegation is recorded, enabling joint evaluation of deliverable quality and the organization of the underlying work. Experiments with nine models show that no single configuration performs best across all domains and that systems exhibit distinct delegation strategies: at high effort, Claude models in Claude Code invoke workflows less frequently but with larger worker groups, whereas GPT models in Codex delegate more frequently in smaller units. When the executing model is held fixed on a challenging subset of tasks, workflows authored by Claude Opus 5.5 substantially improve weaker executors, indicating that workflow organization is itself a measurable determinant of task performance.
title: WorkflowArena: Benchmarking Executable Workflow Orchestration in LLM-Based Multi-Agent Systems

summary: Cryptocurrency markets provide a natural testbed for autonomous AI agents because they are digital-native, high-frequency, and machine-speed environments, yet existing methods often struggle with non-stationary market regimes, opaque decisions, and fixed aggregation rules. In this paper, we propose Agent4Crypto, a dual-reflective and market-feedback-aligned multi-agent system. The framework coordinates specialized agents for data collection, analysis, risk assessment, reflection, and trading, synthesizing heterogeneous signals from prices, indicators, news, and charts in an interpretable decision pipeline. Our central design is a trader-centric decision mechanism: three style-specific trader agents, Aggressive, Neutral, and Conservative, generate candidate actions and natural-language rationales from the same market context, while their influence is learned rather than manually fixed. A PPO-based gating policy dynamically allocates trader weights through a dual-reflective feedback process. One reflection stream evaluates post-trade decision quality from realized portfolio outcomes and distills reusable lessons into a Financial ReasoningBank for retrieval in subsequent trader prompts, while the other estimates trader-level counterfactual contribution, indicating which style has recently aligned better with market movements. The PPO state combines Counterfactual Contribution Memory with market features, previous trader weights, and current trader actions, so trader influence adapts across bull, sideways, and bear regimes. Experiments on BTC, ETH, and XRP show that Agent4Crypto improves total return and Sharpe ratio over traditional strategies, machine learning and reinforcement learning baselines, and existing LLM-based trading systems, demonstrating the value of interpretable trader competition and market-feedback-driven adaptation in volatile cryptocurrency markets.
title: Agent4Crypto: A Dual-Reflective and Market-Feedback-Aligned LLM-Based Multi-Agent System for Cryptocurrency Trading

summary: Electric heavy goods vehicle (eHGV) fleet coordination requires each vehicle to choose driving, charging and resting actions whose consequences depend on shared infrastructure. Existing multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) methods mainly represent current states, leaving action-specific futures and resource interactions to be learned indirectly. We develop Horizon-Preview and Graph-Coordinated Proximal Policy Optimisation (HGC-PPO), which integrates horizon preview and candidate-resource graph coordination into the PPO decision architecture. Horizon preview represents each legal action through its short-horizon operational consequences. Graph message passing then updates these candidates through station, charger-type and time-slot resources shared across the fleet. On the 794km Folkestone-Glasgow task, HGC-PPO achieved the lowest mean charging cost among five RL methods at £504.32 per vehicle, with a fleet completion time of 24.920h. It also completed the task 1.763h faster and cost £36.51 less per vehicle than a replay-verified finite-budget MILP benchmark. Across six unseen routes and fleet sizes from 5 to 20 vehicles, HGC-PPO delivered the lowest macro-average completion time, charging cost and charging frequency among the RL methods. A 2 by 2 ablation showed that the full preview-graph architecture performed best across all four operational metrics. These results show that prospective action information and fleet-wide resource coordination improve eHGV decisions under charging and driver-hours constraints.
title: Prospective Action-Resource Graph Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for Electric HGV Fleets under Shared Charging Infrastructure

summary: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly operate in groups, each pursuing an individual objective while jointly determining system performance. If an operator controls which agent observes which other agent, but not their payoffs or messages, how should observations be structured to raise collective welfare? We make the information network (who observes whom) a design object, decoupled from the fixed interaction network over which agents act. Ten identical LLM agents play repeated group-decision games; by default each observes only an anonymous summary of the group's previous-round outcome, and a manager with a fixed budget adds directed observation links that reveal peers' past actions. Across 1,080 episodes and six games spanning coordination, anti-coordination, social dilemmas, and discovery, we ask how much information to share and, at a fixed budget, who should observe whom. Disclosure creates behavioral coupling: observation acts as a contagion channel whose welfare effect depends on the alignment between individually attractive behavior and the collective objective. First, the value of information is alignment-contingent: more peer information tends to help or be neutral when individual behavior is aligned with the collective goal, but under free-riding or congestion externalities it amplifies collectively harmful behavior; in a public-goods game the group does best with no information at all. We read this sign separation as a cross-game regularity within one controlled LLM population, not a model-invariant law. Second, at a fixed budget, who observes whom matters primarily when coupling is harmful: a modular "barbell" that lets sub-populations entrench harmful behavior is reliably the worst wiring, reversing the network-reciprocity intuition from human evolutionary game theory. These results argue against a default of full transparency for agent collectives.
title: Steering Emergent Behavior in Multi-Agent LLM Systems via Information Networks

summary: We built a hybrid multi-agent trading system that combines large language model (LLM) analysts with momentum-based portfolio construction and rule-based execution. Company-news and macroeconomic agents return structured reports to a coordinator that sets stock weights and cash reserves. We evaluate the portfolio engine using its broker-recorded paper account, which operated with deterministic fallbacks, and compare LLM-enabled configurations through retrospective replays. From March 11 to August 28, 2026, the account returned 34.5%, compared with 14.4% for the S&P 500 fund SPY over the same dates. This raw return advantage came with a larger maximum drawdown. Reconstructed policies also finish above matched SPY and QQQ references when assessments are used in the same session or deferred to the next. Design comparisons examine cash authority, selective invocation, and response contracts. A constant-cash control gives a return estimate close to stance-based sizing, and shorter report contracts improve observed parsing but can change recommendations.
title: Inside the Trading Loop: Markets, Models, and Moves with LLM Agents

summary: Frontline sales staff spend much of their day re-coordinating quotes after customers change quantities, ask for discounts or new payment terms, or costs move. We present LoMASA (Local Multi-Agent Sales Assistant), a training-free multi-agent system that runs entirely on one desktop computer. A 35B mixture-of-experts model (System-1) makes each decision in a single forward pass and reads its confidence from the probabilities of the answer options. A 27B dense model (System-2) writes customer replies and escalation briefs and is consulted when System-1 is unsure. Code computes every price, margin and option, and hard pricing rules cannot be overridden. On a test split of 500 simulated episodes with 1512 decisions built from public supply-chain data, the salesperson has to decide only 19.5% of decisions: 38.0% are settled automatically, with a median latency of 2.67 seconds, and 42.5% are escalated to a manager by the hard rules. On the automatically settled decisions LoMASA is as accurate as a rule baseline (0.894 vs.\ 0.894) and makes fewer commitments whose margin later falls below the floor (2.61% vs 4.53%); the price is additional escalations to the manager. Option probabilities are well calibrated without any training, unlike confidence stated in words by the same model. We also report where the design does not help: the 27B model rarely changes a decision.
title: LoMASA: A Local Multi-Agent Sales Assistant with Confidence-Gated Delegation for B2B Quoting

summary: Agentic AI systems extend large language models with tools, memory, retrieval, browser or computer-use interfaces, code execution, external services, and multi-agent coordination. Although these capabilities enable agents to act beyond text generation and perform tasks, they also create attack paths through which adversaries can exploit untrusted content, deceptive metadata, poisoned state, compromised skills, mutable dependencies, or malicious code. Such attacks can manipulate planning and tool use, corrupt memory, abuse code-execution environments, and trigger harmful downstream effects. In this paper, we present a systematic review of malicious attacks targeting agentic AI systems. We screened 186 candidate sources and retained 98. Following independent coding and resolver adjudication, we identified 284 atomic attacks, 452 atomic safeguards, and 660 explicit attack--safeguard relationships. We organize attacks into eight causal-mechanism classes while retaining insertion points, activation conditions, abused capabilities, objectives, impacts, persistence, and evidence as orthogonal dimensions. Our analysis shows that tool, MCP, and action-layer attacks account for the largest share of atomic attacks, while the prompt-injection and action-hijacking class has the broadest paper coverage. We identify distinct class-specific activation patterns and separation between insertion and later activation. Safeguard coverage remains uneven: only 278 of 660 relationships are directly assessed, and strong coverage is uncommon. These findings support lifecycle-aware threat modeling, agent evaluation, tool governance, and defense-in-depth security for agentic AI systems.
title: Agents of Chaos: A Systematization of Knowledge (SoK) on Malicious Attacks on Agentic AI Systems

summary: Conflicting stakeholder objectives make it difficult to coordinate investments in urban resilience. We model conflict-driven urban design as a non-zero-sum digital board game in which stakeholder agents allocate scarce resources and balance individual payoffs against shared urban development and resilience objectives. We use multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) to train policies and examine their behavior across three settings. On a 4 x 4 board, learned policies reach about 84% of the total return found by a simulated annealing benchmark. On an 8 x 8 board with spatial and resource constraints, trained agents favor projects that improve resilience in self-play. In a 12 x 12 simulation initialized from historical maps of Tatsumi, Tokyo, trained agents achieve a mean total score of 452.1, compared with 357.3 for a random-policy baseline across 10,000 simulation runs. Gains in adaptability, sustainability, flood resistance, and greenery come with reductions in vitality and density. A human-in-the-loop interface supports replay and lets participants take over stakeholder decisions, providing a testbed for exploring these trade-offs in participatory urban planning.
title: A Gamified Framework for Conflict-Driven Design: Discovering Strategies for Collaborative Resilience with Multi-Agent Learning

summary: Multi-agent search and coverage is critical to autonomous exploration, search-and-rescue, and defense applications. This paper investigates settings where a mobile sensor network is tasked with coordinating to discover the position of a stationary target within a bounded region. We develop a Bayesian update scheme where agents iteratively combine local uncertainties derived from their sensor measurements through inverse variance weighting to get a better global understanding of where the target may be located given some prior belief. Network agents' trajectories are governed by a primal-dual gradient update rule that simultaneously minimizes the expected sensing uncertainty and enforces network connectivity among the agents. We prove that the belief converges to the target under mild planner conditions, with an explicit exponential rate of false-hypothesis rejection and a bound on expected search time. Simulation results show that we can successfully find the target and collapse belief to the ground truth target location while ensuring connectivity of our sensor network. They also empirically confirm our theoretical bounds and planner conditions. Finally, we compare against a naive lawnmower sweeping strategy, showing that our method locates the target more quickly when the prior is informative.
title: Belief-Driven Search in Connectivity-Constrained Mobile Sensor Networks with Convergence Guarantees

summary: Networked multi-agent systems coordinating in adversarial environments face compound cyber threats that alternate between false-data injection (FDI), denial-of-service (DoS), and stealthy decoy perturbations designed to mimic benign operational anomalies. Because the switching policy is latent and the plant dynamics evolve continuously, deterministic threshold detectors struggle to isolate deception without causing excessive false alarms. This paper presents an online, data-driven framework that couples distributed continuous time unknown input observers (UIOs) with a topology-aware Hidden Markov Model (HMM) for real-time attack detection and classification under unknown adversarial strategies. By decoupling FDI signals from augmented node states, distributed observers deployed across the network generate local augmented residuals that are discretized into emission sequences. The HMM embeds the underlying directed communication graph into the off-diagonal blocks of its transition probability matrix, explicitly capturing inter-agent attack propagation. Both transition and observation probabilities are updated recursively online via an Expectation-Maximization (EM) scheme, adapting the classifier to evolving threat behaviours without prior offline calibration. Numerical simulations on a directed network demonstrate that incorporating graph topology into the latent transition dynamics resolves the severe classification ambiguity between nominal and decoy modes, outperforming decoupled agent-independent decoders while restricting observer deployment to a sparse subset of nodes.
title: Real-Time Threat Classification in Multi-Agent Systems via Topology-Coupled Hidden Markov Models

summary: Large language models can generate motion graphics from static images and natural language requests, but it remains difficult to evaluate how well models can follow requests that combine spatial, appearance, and temporal requirements. We introduce MotionGraphicsBench, an expert-curated benchmark of 100 instances for animating an input static SVG with a motion edit prompt. By supplying all required visual elements, our editing task reflects a designer-like workflow and isolates motion generation from graphic generation. Derived from real-world Lottie motion designs, our benchmark contains diverse combinations of spatio-temporal animation behaviors. Each benchmark instance pairs its model input with a deterministic, human-readable verification program that accepts different valid implementations and reports which prompt requirements pass or fail, rather than comparing against a reference animation or using a VLM judge. We construct these programs with a multi-agent pipeline using human-labeled animations and synthesized test cases. On a balanced test set of 180 animations, our programs achieve 93.3% raw agreement with human judgments, compared with 83.3% for a GPT-6 Astra VLM baseline, and outperform the baseline in both approval and rejection recall. Across 47 configurations from 32 LLMs and 12 providers, pass@1 ranges from 6.0% to 67.7%. Across 15 models evaluated at their highest available reasoning effort with 32 attempts per instance, additional attempts improve every model, but pass@32 still ranges from 38.0% to 95.0%. Our analysis of verification programs reveals that generated animations often fail to match reference poses, follow requested motion trajectories, or coordinate related events. We release our benchmark at https://huggingface.co/datasets/figma-ai/motion-graphics-bench.
title: MotionGraphicsBench: Evaluating Motion Graphics Generation with Programmatic Verification
