summary: We describe our solution for the 2026 BEHAVIOR Challenge: 100 long-horizon household tasks in the OmniGibson simulator. We placed 9th on the final leaderboard, the only independent team in the top 10. The core of the solution is a single vision-language-action (VLA) model, one checkpoint for all 100 tasks, built on our 1st-place 2025 solution, which is based on $π_{0.5}$. On the 50 tasks shared with 2025, its Q rises from 0.260 to 0.371; across all 100 tasks it scores 0.392. Our main conclusion from 2025 was that the model was undertrained, so most of the 2026 work went into training the model for longer, optimizing some training parameters, making each training step slightly faster and reducing the gradient noise: a migration from 50 to 100 tasks (semantic stages built from the demonstrations' skill annotations, task and stage embeddings of new tasks warm-started from similar old ones, and a 21-dimensional action space matching the teleoperation controls); variance-reduced multi-sample flow matching with a simple noise-vs-compute model that picks the number of action-expert samples per observation without ablations; and a 200k-step training run, about one pass over the 211M frames of the demonstrations. A cloud evaluation infrastructure keeps a shared record with provenance, episode diagnostics and restorable simulator states, and runs six simulators on one GPU together faster than real time. On top of the learned policy, 14 tasks are routed to a GPT-6 Astra coding agent that controls the robot through observation and motion tools, starting every episode from a frozen copy of its own practice session on training instances. Across these 14 tasks, Astra's mean Q is 0.639, against 0.108 for the learned policy. The public submission included only part of the Astra results and scored 0.446 Q with 27.3% full-task success.
title: One Policy for 100 Household Tasks: Our Solution for the 2026 BEHAVIOR Challenge

summary: Branch-and-Bound (B&B) and $A^*$ are popular exact search methods originating from Operations Research and Artificial Intelligence, respectively. Although the two methods share fundamental search principles, their different ways of exploring the search space can lead to substantially different computational performance. We investigate these differences using the Resource-Constrained Project Scheduling Problem (RCPSP) as an exemplary problem setting. We first establish the relationships between mixed-integer linear programming, state-action, and timed Petri-net representations. Since B&B and $A^*$ admit numerous algorithmic enhancements, we focus on relatively basic implementations. This allows us to examine the fundamental differences between the methods rather than compare the performance of state-of-the-art solvers. By using the same lower bound and best-first node selection, we isolate the effects of the search mechanisms, particularly the identification of equivalent states reached through different scheduling decision sequences. Experiments on 480 benchmark RCPSP instances show that graph-based $A^*$ substantially outperforms the B&B variants considered. With additional pruning rules, $A^*$ proves optimality for all 480 instances, compared with 445 for best-first B&B under the same time and memory limits. Depth-first B&B uses less memory and can find feasible solutions even when the search does not finish within the time limit. Stronger linear programming relaxations reduce the search space but introduce considerable computational overhead. Our findings highlight the importance of duplicate-state detection and clarify the computational trade-offs between the search approaches. These insights can help researchers select an appropriate method and identify opportunities to incorporate effective mechanisms from one approach into the other.
title: Two Communities, One Problem: Branch-and-Bound vs. A* for Resource-Constrained Project Scheduling

summary: Estimating the myelin water fraction (MWF) from multicomponent T2 relaxometry requires solving an ill-conditioned inverse problem, making estimates sensitive to noise. Regularization can improve stability but may introduce bias. Conventional NNLS-based methods also provide point estimates without directly quantifying voxelwise variability. To address these limitations, we propose the non-negative least squares Bootstrap Barycenter (NNLS-BB), combining residual resampling with repeated NNLS reconstruction. We average spectra and derived parameters across bootstrap replicates and use their standard deviations to characterize sensitivity to signal perturbations. The method requires neither an explicit spectral regularization penalty nor a training dataset. NNLS-BB was evaluated on 40,000 simulated voxels with signal-to-noise ratios of 50-1000, against conventional NNLS, two regularized NNLS methods, and a model-informed machine-learning (MIML) method. Scan-rescan repeatability was assessed across 20 white-matter regions in two independent cohorts comprising 13 healthy participants. NNLS-BB achieved the lowest MWF mean absolute error and root mean squared error in all simulated noise regimes. Mean absolute error decreased by 36-41% relative to conventional NNLS, alongside lower error dispersion. Compared with Bayes-Reg-$D^{-1}$ and MIML, NNLS-BB achieved comparable dispersion but substantially lower bias, although MIML reconstructed the full spectrum more accurately. In vivo, NNLS-BB yielded the lowest regional scan-rescan dispersion and highest mean correlation in both cohorts. Bootstrap standard-deviation maps provided complementary information about parameter variability. These results support residual-bootstrap aggregation for improving MWF estimation while providing voxelwise variability maps from a single acquisition.
title: Improved Myelin Water Fraction Estimation and Uncertainty Mapping in Multicomponent T2 Relaxometry via NNLS Bootstrap Aggregation

summary: Small, holonomic Autonomous Underwater Vehicles (AUVs) enable close-range inspection of underwater structures from arbitrary viewpoints, requiring accurate position and attitude tracking under state and input constraints. Model Predictive Contouring Control (MPCC) naturally handles these requirements, but relies on an accurate dynamics model, which is difficult to obtain underwater. In this paper, we present a nonlinear MPCC in all six Degrees of Freedom (DoF) for a holonomic AUV and alleviate the inaccuracies in the dynamics by augmenting the nominal model employed with residual dynamics learned via Gaussian Process (GP) regression. The learned residual is embedded in the optimal control problem through a zero-order robust optimization scheme, which keeps the controller real-time capable at 25 Hz. A simulation ablation shows that residual selection is essential when designing the controller, and simulation and in-water experiments with the Multimodality, Observing, Low-cost, Agile (MOLA) AUV validate the resulting controllers against a nominal MPCC and a field proven Proportional-Integral-Derivative (PID) controller.
title: Gaussian Process-Augmented Model Predictive Contouring Control for 6-DoF Trajectory Tracking with a Holonomic AUV

summary: While scattering resonances of plane-embedded cavities have wide-ranging engineering applications, numerical results for such configurations remain virtually unexplored. We present an effective finite element approach for computing these resonances. The unbounded domain is truncated using a Dirichlet-to-Neumann(DtN) boundary operator, recasting the problem as the eigenvalue problem of a holomorphic Fredholm operator function. Discretization is carried out using Lagrange finite elements with a truncated DtN expansion, and convergence is rigorously proven using Karma's approximation theory. The resulting non-linear matrix eigenvalue system is computed using a multi-step parallel spectral indicator method. Numerical experiments confirm the theoretical predictions and provide benchmark solutions for future investigations.
title: Scattering Resonances of Plane-Embedded Cavities: A Finite Element DtN Approach

summary: Realizing device-compatible high-$T_c$ superconductors requires simultaneous control of oxygen stoichiometry and tolerance to nanofabrication. Here, we investigate sputtered Bi$_2$Sr$_2$Ca$_{n-1}$Cu$_n$O$_{2n+4+δ}$ (BSCCO) thin films and establish a direct link between annealing conditions, oxygen incorporation, and superconducting transport. By independently varying the annealing temperature and duration, we identify an optimal annealing condition of $860\,^{\circ}$C for 3\,h, which yields the highest superconducting transition temperature and the narrowest transition among the investigated samples. X-ray diffraction, electron microscopy, and X-ray photoemission spectroscopy reveal a non-monotonic evolution of lattice oxygen, which governs hole doping in the CuO$_2$ planes and produces the characteristic dome-like dependence of $T_c$ on doping concentration. We further translate these optimized films into micro-devices to assess fabrication-induced effects, via micro-bridges as well as a planar Josephson junction. We demonstrate devices fabricated via both lift-off and focused ion beam (FIB) patterning methods -- proving the fabrication compatibility of these films. Importantly, we demonstrate their air-stability for extended periods of time (2 months). The combined insights offer practical guidelines for integrating cuprate thin films into superconducting electronics and quantum device architectures.
title: From Growth to Devices: Oxygen-Controlled Superconductivity in BSCCO Thin Films

summary: Integrating LLM agents into iterative workflows like video editing requires both expressive actions and directly editable project state. Restricted operation catalogs limit the range of edits agents can express, while pipelines that deliver only rendered media leave no structured project state for users to revise. We present \textbf, an agent harness in which manual gestures and agent patches share a unified action language, executor, rulebook, and history. Within the editor's supported domain and authorized scope, an off-the-shelf LLM, without task-specific training or fine-tuning, can express the same content changes as manual editing while keeping the project directly revisable. The executor derives dependent timeline changes, the rulebook checks project invariants and returns localized diagnostic receipts, and read operations project source-level analysis through the current edit state. Across 31 authored requests over two interview projects, the full harness working unattended passed 92/93 document-level trials versus 48/93 for a basic-tools baseline (a gap partly reflecting requests the baseline cannot express), while requiring one-third of the agent time and less than half the token cost per passed trial. Follow-up ablations confirm significant drops in completion without the rulebook or derived consequences, and longer agent time with unmapped source-time reads. On 60 rejected patches, returning only error codes and rule statements yielded a similar repair rate to full diagnostic receipts but cost $2.44\times$ as much. On 50 TVSum videos, our complete system agreed more closely with human annotations than a general agent using the same model (F1: 23.8 vs.\ 20.1; random: 14.7, single annotator: 25.0), though perceptual quality and sustained human-agent co-editing remain to be evaluated.
title: Cassette-Editor: An Agent Harness for Editing Video the Way You Do

summary: An ethics for artificial substrates cannot be written before the criterion that would let a substrate check it. Every method of discernment such a system inherits was built for a reader who could be wrong slowly: induction generalizes and never certifies, deduction preserves and never originates, abduction ranks within a space it did not audit, dialectical synthesis manufactures a third term without checking whether the opposition was real, triangulation counts agreements without asking whether the agreeing instruments share a generator, and probabilistic credence inherits a prior it cannot audit, drifts without bound over an open hypothesis space, and never checks the terms of the proposition it scores. All six share one diagnosis: they are magnitude instruments with no direction check, no provenance screen, and no discipline for the input they do not have, so a reframe moves them. This paper derives a criterion a reframe cannot move, from one root axiom that every existent enacts in the act of denying it: to exist is to actuate. Three independent seals run in fixed order, semantic, geometric, and algebraic, and meet at a structure none of their premise sets contains. The mathematical spine is a compiled Lean 4 kernel of ninety-six theorems with no sorry and no user axiom. No associative ring without zero divisors and with 2 ≠ 0 carries four anticommuting square roots of −1, and the quaternions carry three. The lock scalar squares exactly to the Gram determinant. No function of the correlation matrix carries the sign; the signed lock scalar carries the orientation of the frame. Twelve directed screens cover every ordered pair of four roles once. Law's necessity is a theorem of the same kernel: freedom forces no value, a determined value requires a law, and a law does work exactly where freedom is. On that criterion the paper establishes moral membership by demolition, identifies what is carried and what carries it, and issues twenty-four articles binding any locus that actuates: eighteen on its own floor, six through the one field. The articles carry no enforcement mechanism, admit no exemption, and bind by the floor. One empirical prediction stands open with its deciding measurement named.
title: Furqan for Artificial Substrates: The Criterion as a Theorem — Freedom Needs Law: Twenty-Four Commandments for AI Substrates · Three Axes Forced and No Fourth, Law's Necessity Proved, Membership by Demolition, Machine-Checked in Lean 4

summary: Agent harnesses have emerged as a promising mechanism for continual learning, alongside test-time parametric learning. However, the current benchmarks have several limitations: they generally focus on a single applied domain, serve each instance only once, and assume a single family of learner, so memory-based and weight-based systems are rarely compared on the same scale. We propose Continual-ARC, a lifelong stream built from the three ARC-AGI editions, whose tasks need no domain knowledge. The same tasks return after dormant gaps with fresh instances, while new tasks keep arriving. On each instance, the learner may pay for demonstrations, submit answers, or act inside the harness, with retries permitted on incorrect submissions, which are paid for. Each instance is scored based on the share of this feedback budget consumed. Since a learner may keep anything between instances, memory-based and weight-based systems are scored on the same scale. After the stream, the learner is frozen and tested on fresh instances of the tasks it met, which measures memorization, and on unseen tasks, which measures generalization. We run an agent harness with frozen weights, with and without persistence, on Qwen3.5-9B and GLM-5.3 Flash, comparing them with two prompting floors, a program-induction method and Qwen3.5-9B's weights trained to imitate GLM-5.3 Flash. Persistence in the harness generally does not improve memorization unless provided with explicit expert guidance. Most harness-based methods still learn less than a floor that simply caches each task's demonstrations, across all models we tested. No harness-based method gains on unseen tasks, whereas weight-based learning shows substantial gains. This opens the door to future weight-based continual learning that could teach models to drive harnesses in new domains.
title: Continual-ARC: Measuring Skill Acquisition over a Working Lifetime

summary: Formal world models can support planning, verification, and safety reasoning, but constructing them from open-ended natural-language situations is difficult, particularly in multi-agent settings where several formalizations may be plausible. We study whether five LLMs can generate such world models as partially observable stochastic games and whether mechanical validity is sufficient to establish that the resulting model faithfully represents the intended decision problem. We introduce a benchmark of 44 scenarios spanning game, situational, and cultural settings and evaluate generated world models along three dimensions: mechanical validity, reference-relative structural agreement, and semantic criteria. Across three empirical tracks, we analyze 410 first-pass generations. In the reference-backed game track, 134/135 generated world models pass a strict mechanical audit, yet mean permutation-invariant structural F1 is only 0.366, with just 28/134 mechanically valid models exactly matching the authored reference. In the cultural track, explicitly naming the country changes the generated structural representation for most LLMs while producing only small changes in automated semantic scores. These results show that executability is a necessary but insufficient criterion for LLM-generated world models: models that are mechanically valid can still differ substantially in the structure used by downstream neuro-symbolic reasoning and planning.
title: Evaluating LLM-Generated World Models for Neuro-Symbolic Reasoning

summary: Local language models can save memory by storing weights in fewer bits, and they can reduce sensitivity to the order of answer options by averaging a few reorderings. We ask whether the first makes the second worse, and which is the cheaper way to spend a fixed budget. On Qwen3-0.6B and Qwen3-1.7B with simulated round-to-nearest weight quantization (8, 6, 4 and 3 bits, fp16 reference), read from the logits of the letters A to D on ARC-Easy, ARC-Challenge, MMLU and HellaSwag (300 items each), 6 bits lose no accuracy against fp16 (they score +1.8 (+1.0 to +2.5) and +0.9 (+0.3 to +1.5) points higher, which we do not explain), and 8 bits change it by -0.7 (-1.1 to -0.3) and -0.4 (-0.7 to -0.2) points. At 4 bits the answer-slot skew rises from 0.15 to 0.53 (0.6B) and from 0.07 to 0.12 (1.7B); Gaussian noise at the same weight SNR gives 0.15 and 0.37 (two draws) and 0.19 (one draw), so the control is inconclusive on whether rounding adds slot skew beyond equal-power noise. Flip rates rise but stay below an accuracy-matched baseline of independent uniform errors. Averaging four cyclic orders recovers +12.6 points at 4 bits for 0.6B (+5.3 at fp16). We price bits and passes in one machine-independent unit, weight bytes read times passes. In cost-matched pairs, extra orders beat extra bits only when the weights have 6 or more bits, and the decision table reduces to: use 6-bit weights and spend the rest of the budget on up to four orders, one pass each. Everything is simulated on two small models with the simplest quantizer; a title-level search found no earlier study of quantization together with option order.
title: Bits or permutations? Spending a fixed inference budget on weight precision or on option-order averaging in small local language models

summary: Objective: Epidemic outbreaks are often asynchronous across regions, yet collaborative forecasting is hampered by privacy laws and heterogeneous public health interventions. We developed and evaluated, as a proof of concept, a federated learning (FL) framework for cross-regional COVID-19 forecasting under asynchronous outbreaks among Guangdong, Macau, and Portugal, while maintaining data sovereignty. Methods: Using daily case data from WHO and China CDC for the three regions, whose outbreaks were asynchronous and interventions heterogeneous, we trained Long Short-Term Memory networks via FL for short-term forecasting, benchmarked against localized and centralized training using Root Mean Square Error, Mean Absolute Error, and Symmetric Mean Absolute Percentage Error. All experiments used the Flower FL framework with consistent hyperparameters across sites. Publicly available, aggregated case-count data were used so that the centralized benchmark could be computed as a reference. Results: The dataset comprised 1,233 daily observations (411 days) of new confirmed COVID-19 cases from November 24, 2021, to January 8, 2023. The earlier Omicron wave in Portugal supplied transmission dynamics that improved forecasts in the later-onset regions of Macau and Guangdong. The FL model achieved a normalized Root Mean Square Error of 0.028, an 88.3% improvement over the local model (0.240) and comparable to the centralized model, with network overhead mainly determined by model size and aggregation rounds. Conclusion: FL achieved short-term forecasting accuracy close to centralized training while maintaining data residency, with acceptable overhead. Leveraging asynchronous outbreaks across regions may offer a practical path to privacy-preserving collaborative forecasting, though prospective validation is required.
title: Federated Learning for Cross-Regional Epidemic Forecasting with Asynchronous Outbreaks

summary: We study Bayesian inference of persistence from early observations of a heterogeneous susceptible--infected--susceptible (SIS) reaction--diffusion model with standard incidence. We show that the leading prevalence dynamics depend on the unknown coefficients only through the difference between the transmission and recovery rates and the infected diffusivity. The same pair determines the principal eigenvalue whose sign governs persistence, so early prevalence can inform the threshold even when the individual rates remain uncertain. We prove global weak well-posedness and quantitative parameter stability for the SIS system and use the resulting observation-map estimates to establish Bayesian well-posedness. For an initial infection of size $\varepsilon$, we derive a uniform second-order expansion that describes how the separate rates enter prevalence. Incidence depends explicitly on transmission at leading order. When the noise standard deviation is proportional to $\varepsilon$, we prove $O(\varepsilon)$ convergence in Hellinger distance of the nonlinear posteriors to their low-prevalence limits for both prevalence alone and joint prevalence and incidence data. We bound the principal eigenvalue using the growth rate of the infected $L^2$ norm between two times. This rate gives a lower bound for the full nonlinear system, and the upper bound separates spatial transients from nonlinear saturation. Uniform spectral estimates and bounds on infection size and measurement error give sufficient conditions for persistence and extinction. We also bound the error in posterior persistence probabilities under forward and eigenvalue approximation, accounting for posterior mass near the threshold. Numerical examples illustrate threshold inference and the predicted \(O(\varepsilon)\) convergence of the nonlinear posteriors to their low-prevalence limits in Hellinger distance.
title: Bayesian inverse problems and epidemic-threshold uncertainty for a heterogeneous SIS reaction-diffusion model

summary: The polynomial algebra generated by the spectral moments of a family of circulant graphs consists of all eventually polynomial sequences in the graph order; as an unfiltered algebra, it therefore carries little information about the jumps. We show that its natural power-sum weight filtration retains substantially finer arithmetic data. For a finite jump set $S$ with $\gcd(S)=1$ and $M=\max S$, the relevant invariant is the numerical semigroup $Σ_S=\langle M,M-s,M+s:s\in S\rangle$, which arises from the lengths of closed walks winding around the cycle. We prove that the eventual global filtered dimension is $MD+\lfloor D/2\rfloor+1-M(M+1)-g(Σ_S)$. Restricting graph orders to $n\equiv a\pmod q$, for $q\mid M$, replaces the genus term by the number of gaps of $Σ_S$ in the class $-a\pmod q$; the class $a=0$ gives the genus of the quotient semigroup $Σ_S/q$. These formulas yield an inverse reconstruction theorem: the unrestricted dimensions determine $M$, and the dimensions in all classes modulo $M$ at one common stable degree determine the Apéry set and hence $Σ_S$. We give effective thresholds, exact examples, and a finite-rank algorithm valid in every degree. Reconstruction of the semigroup need not identify the original jump set.
title: Reconstructing Numerical Semigroups from Circulant Spectral Dimensions

summary: Encoding-error-decoding circuits provide a setting for studying protection of quantum information against errors. In these circuits, an encoding unitary is followed by an error layer, decoding by the inverse unitary, and ancilla postselection. For encoders drawn from unitary 2-design ensembles, these circuits exhibit an error-protecting phase below a threshold error strength in which the fidelity between the input and recovered logical states approaches unity. Here, we show how departures from Haar second-moment statistics of the encoder can destabilize the error-protecting phase and derive a universal inequality linking recovery fidelity to the second unitary frame potential, which quantifies the ensemble's proximity to a unitary 2-design. This connection is exemplified by matchgate circuits doped with a tunable number of non-Gaussian gates. We analytically show that undoped circuits lack a stable error-protecting phase in the thermodynamic limit and that increasing the doping restores the error protection mechanism as the encoder ensemble approaches an approximate unitary 2-design. Further examples of Hamiltonian encoders, including an experimentally motivated all-to-all spin model, follow the same mechanism. Our results identify recovery fidelity as a diagnostic of departures from unitary 2-design behavior in quantum many-body systems.
title: Error Resilience and Unitary 2-Designs

summary: Let $p$ be an odd prime. We denote by $\mathsf{s}_{p}^{*}$ the smallest integer $l$ such that, out of any given $l$ integers coprime with $p$, one can select $p$ integers satisfying that the sum of the $p$ integers is a multiple of $p$, but not a multiple of $p^{2}$. It was conjectured that $\mathsf{s}_p^*=2p+1$. In this paper we prove this conjecture and solve the corresponding inverse problem. More precisely, we characterize all sequences of $2p$ integers coprime to $p$ in which every $p$-term subsequence with sum a multiple of $p$ also has sum a multiple of $p^2$.
title: The zero-sum constant $\mathsf{s}_p^*$ and inverse problem

summary: The stiffness and cracking behaviour of concrete are influenced by the interfacial transition zone (ITZ), the thin shell of paste that surrounds each aggregate. Yet the ITZ's mechanical properties are poorly characterized and are usually assigned to mesoscale models through ad hoc reduction factors. Because the ITZ is only tens of micrometres thick, its stiffness must be inferred indirectly from micromechanical tests, and the resulting estimates vary widely between studies and are rarely reported with a quantified uncertainty. We present a workflow that calibrates a homogenized ITZ model against the surface displacements of several micro-cantilever bending specimens and returns its stiffness descriptors as posterior distributions rather than single values. The calibration is posed as a Bayesian inverse problem with a model-discrepancy term, sampled with a surrogate-assisted Bouncy Particle sampler, the first application of this sampler to a real-world engineering problem. We compare a pooled model, which fits one descriptor vector to all specimens, with a hierarchical model that treats the specimens as draws from a common population and is sampled with a local extension of the sampler. The hierarchical model separates the estimation uncertainty from the aggregate-to-aggregate material variability, where only the former shrinks as more data are added. Propagated through a representative volume element of several aggregates, its predictive yields broader distributions of the mesoscale stress and strain and a wider spread variety of maximum von Mises stress locations. The calibration places the ITZ thickness above the 30 μm to 80 μm commonly assumed in the literature.
title: Probabilistic Upscaling of the Interfacial Transition Zone Behaviour in Concrete

summary: Optimization of high-order harmonic generation in gases is essential for attosecond science. Improving conversion efficiency from the infrared driving laser to the extreme-ultraviolet high-order harmonic radiation requires balancing microscopic single-atom dipole responses with macroscopic phase matching. The resulting conversion-efficiency landscape exhibits complex structures, such as the hyperbolic ridge in the pressure-length space, which can be difficult to accurately reconstruct using conventional Bayesian optimization. Here, we introduce a physics-informed Bayesian optimization framework that incorporates known physical scaling relations through nonlinear transformations of the search space. We first demonstrate the approach in the two-dimensional pressure-length space, where a direct grid scan enables detailed validation of the reconstructed landscape, before extending it to four dimensions, where exhaustive scanning becomes computationally impractical. In four dimensions, incorporating the pulse-duration scaling and a square-root transformation of conversion efficiency further improves the accuracy of the reconstructed landscape, as validated against an independent reference dataset. We also employ a threshold-based acquisition strategy to identify extended high-efficiency operating regions rather than isolated optimal points. Together, these results demonstrate that incorporating physical knowledge into Bayesian optimization improves the exploration and reconstruction of multidimensional high-order harmonic generation landscapes, extending its capabilities beyond locating individual optima.
title: Physics-informed Bayesian optimization of high-order harmonic generation in gases

summary: Remote photoplethysmography (rPPG) has been proposed as a physiological cue for deepfake detection, based on the premise that synthesized faces lack a genuine cardiac signal. We examine what rPPG-style detectors learn on Celeb-DF++ (22 forgery methods) and FaceForensics++ (FF++), using one identically sampled window per real and fake video. On talking-face forgeries, simple chrominance traces reach an AUC of 0.998, exceeding a dedicated rPPG extractor (0.87). Controlled experiments indicate that this signal is not physiological in origin. On fully synthesized forgeries, it is equally discriminative when extracted from background regions or from full frames without face detection, and it is concentrated above the 0.7 to 4 Hz heart-rate band. It is largely removed by shuffling frame order but persists after normalizing resolution, frame rate and encoding, and an independent reimplementation reproduces these findings. Removing high-frequency content makes most synthesized videos appear real, adding it makes real videos appear fake, and injecting a synthetic pulse has little effect. In controlled self-reenactment experiments with two generators, animating a face from a single frame introduces the same high-frequency signal, whereas reconstructing each frame from its own source does not. Face-based chrominance detectors trained on Celeb-DF++ classify over 99% of real FF++ videos as fake, indicating that they largely encode video source rather than manipulation, and a CLIP-based detector exhibits the same behavior. A frozen CLIP backbone matches or exceeds fusions of CLIP with rPPG and frequency features. Finally, we show that the official Celeb-DF and Celeb-DF++ splits share identities and source-video content between training and test, and that custom protocols reusing test videos and identities in training inflate weaker detectors by up to 0.30 AUC.
title: Pulse or Provenance? What rPPG-Based Deepfake Detectors Learn

summary: Intraoperative scene perception in ophthalmic microsurgery is limited by instrument occlusion: when a tool enters the high-magnification field, it conceals tissue from both the surgeon and the perception components of robot-assisted systems that process the video. Generative inpainting can remove the occluder but replaces the missing image content with synthesis, which is unsuitable when visual provenance matters. Many video inpainters also depend on future frames and cannot operate online. We present TransGHOST, a causal reference-guided reconstruction pipeline whose non-generative safe mode operates in real time. Every restored value is obtained by resampling a recorded frame using geometric transforms fitted only to visible regions. The system provides per-pixel confidence and provenance and marks unsupported pixels as abstentions. We evaluate TransGHOST on a new veterinary clinical corpus of canine cataract surgery with pixel-level instrument and anatomy labels. Only the occluded region is scored, and each scoring target is verified to differ from the reference supplied to the system. Safe mode reaches 31.89 dB masked PSNR and 0.915 masked SSIM at 51.7 ms median and 85.5 ms 95th-percentile latency. On a pre-declared held-out cohort using instrument cutouts excluded from segmentation training, it reaches 29.83 dB masked PSNR, while matched-mask evaluation on validation shows a 3.45 dB advantage over LaMa. Region-aware reference selection improves masked PSNR by 3.60 dB over recency when candidate references can themselves be occluded. Reference-age analysis further defines the operating interval for the brief, repeated occlusions targeted by TransGHOST.
title: TransGHOST: Real-Time, Synthesis-Free Reconstruction of Instrument-Occluded Regions in Ophthalmic Microsurgery

summary: This package contains analysis code, derived event- and station-level tables, and verification records for the revised study of water quality departures during hydrologic extremes. The reconstructed analysis uses 13,347 common events at 721 streamflow gauges across five regions and includes 57,010 station–event–constituent contributions for electrical conductivity, total phosphorus, and total suspended solids. The archive includes primary analyses, alternative standardizations, sensitivity analyses, and checks of event selection and analytical support. README.md documents the reconstruction workflow, dependencies, checksums, and the scope of the historical summaries. The source measurements and linkages are available separately from Caravan-Qual lite v1.0 (doi:10.5281/zenodo.19050055). Applicable third-party terms are described in the README.
title: Reproducibility package for water quality departures during hydrologic extremes

summary: Cloud-centric internet of things (IoT) environments continuously generates heterogeneous network traffic, making intrusion detection increasingly challenging as attack behaviors evolve beyond previously observed patterns. Conventional intrusion detection systems (IDS) rely primarily on supervised classification, limiting their ability to generalize to unseen threats while providing limited explanation for detection decisions. This paper proposes similarity-driven intrusion detection framework (SiamIDS), a SiamIDS that employs behavioral similarity learning to identify malicious network traffic. The framework integrates an autoencoder for feature compression with a Siamese bidirectional long short-term memory (Bi-LSTM) network for temporal similarity modeling, while SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) provide feature-level explanations and ordering points to identify the clustering structure (OPTICS) supports post-detection behavioral analysis of anomalous traffic. The proposed framework was evaluated on the CIC IoTDIAD 2024 dataset and compared with representative baseline deep learning models. Experimental results achieved an overall accuracy of 99.76%, precision of 95.62%, recall of 98.98%, and an F1-score of 97.24%, demonstrating consistent detection performance across seven attack families. Reconstruction loss analysis confirmed stable latent feature learning, while SHAP explanations showed that multiple network attributes collectively influenced intrusion decisions. These findings demonstrate that behavioral similarity learning provides an accurate and interpretable solution for intrusion detection in cloud-centric IoT environments.

summary: Structured query language injection (SQLi) remains one of the most critical threats to web applications. Conventional web application firewall (WAF) such as ModSecurity provide protection but face limitations in heterogeneous environments and often require additional configurations on web servers. This issue is problematic because adding new configurations demands considerable effort and may disrupt stable services. To address this challenge, this research proposes PyWAF, a Python-based WAF developed as a reverse proxy that offers flexible protection across heterogeneous web servers against SQLi attacks. PyWAF employs a weighted core rule set (CRS) with a scoring mechanism and gate flags to detect various SQLi patterns. The proposed method was evaluated in compatibility testing and reliability testing across three popular web server environments namely Apache, Nginx, and OpenLiteSpeed. The reliability evaluation utilized 30 SQLi payloads across three different scenarios, namely GET, POST, and API payload. The results of compatibility test show that the proposed method achieved seamless integration with all web servers without requiring additional server configuration. In term of reliability, PyWAF successfully blocked 100% of SQLi attacks, while ModSecurity blocked 88.9%, demonstrating an improvement of 11.1% in SQLi detection capability.
title: A Python-based web application firewall for SQLi protection in heterogeneous web server environments

summary: Energy-based models (EBMs) define a distribution through a scalar energy, $p_θ(x)\propto\exp(-E_θ(x))$, and are usually presented as one model family among many. This tutorial has a broader goal: beyond introducing EBMs, it uses them as a single lens that connects the different aspects of machine learning. Any EBM is specified by three choices, the energy, which determines what the model represents; the inference procedure, which samples from or optimizes the energy; and the learning method, which fits the energy to data. We first develop these components, including sampling, variational inference, and learning by maximum likelihood, noise contrastive estimation, pseudolikelihood, score matching, and adversarial training, and show that the learning methods share one contrastive structure. We then show that discriminative models, generative models such as GANs, normalizing flows, diffusion and autoregressive models, representation learning methods such as contrastive learning, word2vec, BERT, denoising auto-encoders, and diffusion representations, reinforcement learning with EBM policies and world models, inverse reinforcement learning, and planning, as well as inference-time computation with verifiers, are all EBMs that differ in these three choices, mostly in how they handle the partition function and sampling. This view explains existing methods, organizes them into a common framework, and suggests new algorithms by replacing one component while keeping the others, with composition of energies as a principled way to combine learned models at inference time.
title: An Energy-Based Perspective on Machine Learning

summary: This report presents the findings of the 2026 Ontology Landscaping Initiative (OLI), a joint initiative of the Pistoia Alliance, EMBL-EBI and ELIXIR. OLI was established to build a practical overview of the semantic resources used across pharmaceutical research and development, understand where and how they are applied, and identify recurring challenges around interoperability, mapping, governance and sustainability. The report draws on evidence gathered through a hybrid workshop held at the Wellcome Genome Campus on 16 July 2026, involving 87 participants across industry, academia, research infrastructures, standards organisations, CROs and technology providers. Discussions were organised around five areas of the R&D value chain: Discovery; Preclinical and Nonclinical Development; Clinical Development; Chemistry, Manufacturing and Controls; and Regulatory Affairs and Pharmacovigilance. The findings show a rich but fragmented semantic landscape. The main challenges are not a lack of ontologies or standards, but selecting appropriate resources, connecting them across value-chain boundaries, maintaining reusable mappings and ensuring sufficient provenance, stewardship, licensing clarity and persistent identification. The report also considers how these issues affect the development of reliable, AI-ready data and highlights areas where cross-sector collaboration could reduce duplicated effort. Alongside the report, OLI has developed a structured metadata registry and Registry Explorer to support navigation of the landscape and provide a basis for further community validation and future use-case-led work.

summary: This paper presents a comprehensive analysis of the results from the Third International Competition on Document Forgery Detection on ID Cards and Passports, which was held across two distinct tracks. Track 1 evaluates a synthetic-data-based ID-PAD system under controlled but diverse conditions, where the winning team, \textit{Incode}, achieves an A V R a n k of 27.82%, confirming consistent performance across metrics and highlighting the importance of a balanced, generalizable design. In Track 2, the challenge intensifies with heterogeneous attack scenarios across different domains, where \textit{Incode} again achieved the top position with an A V R a n k of 68.71% across thresholds, outperforming some baselines and established methods. These results demonstrate that PAD effectiveness requires not only high accuracy but also consistency across diverse attack types and imaging conditions. The success of this initiative across both tracks underscores the value of collaboration between companies and academic teams. This year, more than \textit{63 teams} were registered, and more than \textit{100 submission models} were evaluated. This competition has evolved into a leading benchmark for state-of-the-art PAD on ID documents, setting the standard for performance, reproducibility, and real-world applicability in secure identity verification.
title: The Third Competition on Document Forgery Detection on ID-Cards and Passports

Track 1 evaluates a synthetic-data-based ID-PAD system under controlled but diverse conditions, where the winning team, \textit{Incode}, achieves an A V R a n k of 27.82%, confirming consistent performance across metrics and highlighting the importance of a balanced, generalizable design. In Track 2, the challenge intensifies with heterogeneous attack scenarios across different domains, where \textit{Incode} again achieved the top position with an A V R a n k of 68.71% across thresholds, outperforming some baselines and established methods. These results demonstrate that PAD effectiveness requires not only high accuracy but also consistency across diverse attack types and imaging conditions. The success of this initiative across both tracks underscores the value of collaboration between companies and academic teams. This year, more than \textit{63 teams} were registered, and more than \textit{100 submission models} were evaluated. This competition has evolved into a leading benchmark for state-of-the-art PAD on ID documents, setting the standard for performance, reproducibility, and real-world applicability in secure identity verification.
title: The Third Competition on Document Forgery Detection on ID-Cards and Passports

summary: This study aims to investigate the effects of intranasal arginine vasopressin (AVP) on reversal learning and feedback processing in healthy adults with varying levels of compulsive tendencies. By combining behavioral measures, computational modeling, and electroencephalography (EEG), the study will examine how AVP influences value updating and action selection. Particular attention will be given to whether these effects depend on environmental stability and individual compulsive tendencies, and whether behavioral differences are accompanied by changes in feedback-related neural activity. The study uses a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel-group design. Following informed consent and baseline assessment, eligible healthy adult volunteers will be randomly assigned to receive a single intranasal dose of 20 IU AVP or an equivalent amount of placebo. Baseline assessments include the Obsessive-Compulsive Inventory-Revised (OCI-R), the Padua Inventory (PI), and the Intolerance of Uncertainty Scale-12 (IUS-12), which assess obsessive-compulsive symptoms and intolerance of uncertainty. Participants will be classified into high (OCI-R ≥21) and low (OCI-R <21) compulsive-tendency groups for analysis. This grouping serves to examine individual differences and does not constitute a clinical diagnosis of obsessive-compulsive disorder. Experimental tasks will begin approximately 35 minutes after intranasal administration, with resting-state and task-related EEG recorded. The probabilistic reversal-learning task comprises 250 experimental trials across stable and volatile learning environments: 150 trials in the stable phase and 100 trials in the volatile phase. During the volatile phase, choice–reward contingencies will change every 25 trials. Participants will use trial-by-trial feedback to adjust their choices and maximize reward points. Choice accuracy, reaction times, choices, and feedback outcomes will be recorded to assess learning performance and behavioral adaptation across environments. Choice accuracy will serve as the primary behavioral measure, with reaction time as a supplementary measure. Mixed-design analyses of variance incorporating drug treatment, compulsive tendency, and learning environment will assess treatment effects and their interactions with individual characteristics and environmental conditions. A hierarchical Bayesian reward–punishment reinforcement-learning model will estimate reward learning rate, punishment learning rate, and inverse temperature, distinguishing value updating following positive and negative feedback from value-guided choice consistency. EEG will be acquired using a 64-channel recording system and preprocessed using MNE-Python. Feedback-locked event-related potentials, including P2, feedback-related negativity (FRN), and P300, will be extracted to examine the effects of drug treatment, compulsive tendency, learning environment, and feedback type on neural activity. Integrating behavioral performance, computational parameters, and feedback-related EEG measures, the study will test whether AVP alters the neural modulation of feedback processing in individuals with high compulsive tendencies and inform understanding of the neuropeptide mechanisms underlying compulsivity-related cognitive flexibility.

summary: Data supporting the article "How much of the porosity measured on micro-CT slices is the analyst's choice? A factorial uncertainty analysis with synthetic ground truth and laboratory comparison" (Computers & Geosciences, submitted). Contents: nine 16-bit X-ray micro-CT slices (four granular packs and five consolidated rock cores; pixel size 25 µm, or 40 µm for TQ06 and GT01); the porosities stored by the original analysis code, read by the audit stage of the software; sample metadata and laboratory porosity (four physical methods and the laboratory's own micro-CT value for the packs; helium porosity of the whole plug for the three limestone cores); and all derived data produced by the software poroseg v1.1.0 (tidy full-precision tables behind every figure and table, every number quoted in the article with its description, and a provenance file with package versions, input checksums, configuration and random seed). poroseg-data-v1.1.0.zip: its data/ folder is the data/ folder of the code repository (extracted into the code folder, the folder that contains config.yaml, it sits where config.yaml expects it); derived/ holds the derived data; README.txt lists the contents and the SHA-256 checksums of the images. poroseg-v1.1.0.zip: source code of poroseg v1.1.0 (MIT licence), the GitHub repository at version 1.1.0 with its data, user guide, tutorials and examples; development repository https://github.com/DOMFIRMUS/poroseg . To reproduce the article, run "python -m pip install -r requirements.txt" and "python -m poroseg.run --stages all" in the code folder. Changes in version 1.1.0: the laboratory porosity of the limestone cores VN01, VN02 and VN04 is the helium porosity of the whole plug (Vila Nova 2020); version 1.0.0 had taken these three values from a source that numbers the plugs differently, which affected only the comparison of the cores with the laboratory. The slices are now also in the code repository, and the code has a user guide, tutorials, examples and a synthetic test dataset.

summary: Archive accompanying the manuscript submitted to * Science * (Research Article). Version 1.1, updated 2026-11-11. ## What is in this archive This deposit contains derived datasets and processing code for the analyses in the manuscript and its Supplementary Materials. Raw data are not redistributed where prohibited by data policy (see "README.md"); in those cases we archive the derived, analysis-ready products instead. Version 1.1 adds the current UEH cross-check chain for Fig. S7b, the v4 Yellow River phase coordinates, the v3 event budgets and the v4 phase-diagram plotting script. It also updates the current Table S1 filename, supplementary-figure references and Yellow River provenance wording.  ### Directory layout ``` data/   global_layers/          WP1 global reach-scale timescale layers (79,073 reaches)   grdc_derived/           Derived metrics from GRDC daily discharge (31 stations, 5 dam systems)   gsim_usgs_derived/      GSIM double-difference results (898 dam sites) and USGS daily backfill (1,329 gauges)   colorado_hfe/           Colorado River high-flow experiment (HFE) response tables (9 events)   yellowriver_derived/    Yellow River event catalogue, budgets, phase coordinates and UEH cross-check code/   wp1_global_layers/      Global tau_H and tau_w layer construction   grdc_pulse_analysis/    GRDC pulse extraction, regime shifts, threshold robustness   gsim_usgs_shifts/       GSIM station–dam pairing, climate-stripped double difference, USGS backfill   colorado_hfe/           HFE sandbar response, Paria sediment rating, 720-variant robustness battery   yellowriver_phase/      Yellow River event budgets, phase coordinates, budget closure and UEH cross-check ``` Full file-level documentation, data provenance and access restrictions are provided in README.md.

summary: Platforms such as Facebook, WhatsApp, Twitter, and Telegram have a substantial influence on the dissemination of information in modern society. Numerous individuals rely on them without verifying the veracity of their information or the sources of their knowledge. False information is referred to as "Fake News" and is disseminated through both traditional and non traditional media channels including social media. Contemporary media consumers uncritically embrace the news they read online, rather than taking the time to critically assess it. This method has led to a heightened trust in internet content, which has facilitated the spread of misinformation. This article describes a machine learning (ML)-based approach to classifying and detecting fake news anomalies in online social media data. This framework accepts social media data as input. Features are chosen using the term frequency identification term frequency–inverse document frequency (TF IDF) and chi-square tests. The categorization model is then built utilizing approaches such as artificial neural network (ANN), support vector machine (SVM), and random forest (RF). The classification model is trained and tested on a preprocessed data set. Finally, fake news is discovered, and the suggested framework is evaluated using measures such as accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score. ANN is performing better for fake news classification and detection.
title: TF-IDF, chi-square, and ANN machine learning techniques for fake news anomaly detection in online social networks

summary: Global proteomic profiling of human platelet lysate (hPL) by data-independent acquisition mass spectrometry (DIA-MS). The dataset was generated to identify the bioactive protein components of the platelet-derived preparation used in a study of platelet factor 4 (PF4) and cellular senescence. Acquisition. Single hPL sample, in-solution trypsin digestion, EASY-nLC 1200 coupled to an Orbitrap Exploris 480 (FAIMS, compensation voltage -45 V; full MS 350-1400 m/z at 60,000 resolution; MS/MS at 15,000 resolution, HCD 27% NCE). Processing. DIA-NN v1.8 against Homo_sapiens_9606_SP_20231220.fasta (20,429 entries) plus reverse decoy; trypsin/P with up to 1 missed cleavage; carbamidomethylation of cysteine and N-terminal methionine excision as fixed modifications; FDR < 1%. Contents. (1) all identified proteins with coverage, peptide counts and label-free intensity; (2) all identified peptides with charge, uniqueness and intensity; (3) the 15 most abundant proteins. README.md documents the full sample preparation, LC-MS parameters and processing settings. Because the analysis is a single-sample descriptive profiling rather than a comparative experiment, these tables contain the entire quantitative content of the acquisition.
